questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the righteousness of faith?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that for us to acquire the true knowledge of this great mystery the Holy Spirit kindles in our hearts a true faith that embraces Jesus Christ, with all his merits, and makes him its own, and no longer looks for anything apart from him. For it must necessarily follow that either all that is required for our salvation is not in Christ or, if all is in him, then those who have Christ by faith have his salvation entirely. Therefore, to say that Christ is not enough but that something else is needed as well is a most enormous blasphemy against God- for it then would follow that Jesus Christ is only half a Savior. And therefore we justly say with Paul that we are justified "by faith alone" or "by faith apart from works." (Rom. 3:28) However, we do not mean, properly speaking, that it is faith itself that justifies us- for faith is only the instrument by which we embrace Christ, our righteousness. But Jesus Christ is our righteousness in making available to us all his merits and all the holy works he has done for us and in our place. And faith is the instrument that keeps us in communion with him and with all his benefits. When those benefits are made ours, they are more than enough to absolve us of our sins.

scoring.rubric: Must address the key points of Article 22 (The Righteousness of Faith). Should align with the Belgic Confession's teaching on this topic.

questions.response:
The **Belgic Confession** teaches that the “righteousness of faith” is the righteousness of **Jesus Christ received by faith alone**, not a righteousness produced by our own works or even by faith considered as a meritorious act.

In Articles **22–23**, it teaches that:

- **Faith embraces Jesus Christ** and His merits.
- Christ is our complete righteousness before God.
- We are justified by **faith alone**, because faith is the instrument by which we receive Christ.
- Our sins are forgiven, and Christ’s obedience and righteousness are **imputed** to us.
- We must not trust in our works, even our best works, as the basis of acceptance with God.
- Good works necessarily follow true faith, but they are not the ground of justification.

Article 22 says that faith “embraces Jesus Christ with all His merits” and seeks nothing apart from Him. It also stresses that faith itself does not justify as a work; rather, faith justifies because it receives Christ.

Article 23 explains that our justification consists in the forgiveness of sins and the imputation of Christ’s righteousness. Therefore, believers “always hold fast this foundation,” giving all glory to God and resting entirely on the obedience of Christ crucified.

So, in summary: **the righteousness of faith is Christ’s righteousness counted as ours, received by faith alone, apart from works.**

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the last judgement?
questions.reference_answer: Finally we believe, according to God's Word, that when the time appointed by the Lord is come (which is unknown to all creatures) and the number of the elect is complete, our Lord Jesus Christ will come from heaven, bodily and visibly, as he ascended, with great glory and majesty, to declare himself the judge of the living and the dead. He will burn this old world, in fire and flame, in order to cleanse it. Then all human creatures will appear in person before the great judge- men, women, and children, who have lived from the beginning until the end of the world. They will be summoned there "with the archangel's call and with the sound of God's trumpet." (1 Thess. 4:16) For all those who died before that time will be raised from the earth, their spirits being joined and united with their own bodies in which they lived. And as for those who are still alive, they will not die like the others but will be changed "in the twinkling of an eye" from perishable to imperishable. (1 Cor. 15:51-53) Then the books (that is, the consciences) will be opened, and the dead will be judged according to the things they did in the world, (Rev. 20:12) whether good or evil. Indeed, all people will give account of all the idle words they have spoken, (Matt. 12:36) which the world regards as only playing games. And then the secrets and hypocrisies of all people will be publicly uncovered in the sight of all. Therefore, with good reason the thought of this judgment is horrible and dreadful to wicked and evil people. But it is very pleasant and a great comfort to the righteous and elect, since their total redemption will then be accomplished. They will then receive the fruits of their labor and of the trouble they have suffered; their innocence will be openly recognized by all; and they will see the terrible vengeance that God will bring on the evil ones who tyrannized, oppressed, and tormented them in this world. The evil ones will be convicted by the witness of their own consciences, and shall be made immortal- but only to be tormented in "the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels." (Matt. 25:41) In contrast, the faithful and elect will be crowned with glory and honor. The Son of God will profess their names (Matt. 10:32) before God his Father and the holy and elect angels; all tears will be wiped from their eyes; (Rev. 7:17) and their cause- at present condemned as heretical and evil by many judges and civil officers- will be acknowledged as the cause of the Son of God. And as a gracious reward the Lord will make them possess a glory such as the human heart could never imagine. So we look forward to that great day with longing in order to enjoy fully the promises of God in Christ Jesus, our Lord.

scoring.rubric: Must address the key points of Article 37 (The Last Judgement). Should align with the Belgic Confession's teaching on this topic.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession teaches about the Last Judgement in **Article 37**. In summary, it says:

- **Christ will return visibly and bodily** from heaven, in great glory and majesty, with angels, to judge the living and the dead.
- **The timing is unknown** to all creatures and known only to God; it will occur when the number of the elect is complete.
- **All the dead will be raised**, their souls reunited with their bodies, and those still alive will be changed “in the twinkling of an eye.”
- **All people will appear before Christ**, the great Judge—men, women, and children from the beginning to the end of the world.
- **The books will be opened**, and people will be judged according to what they have done. Even hidden things, hypocrisy, and idle words will be exposed.
- **The wicked and unbelieving** will be condemned by their own consciences and sent to eternal punishment with the devil and his angels.
- **The faithful and elect** will be vindicated, crowned with glory, and receive the gracious reward promised by God. Christ will acknowledge them before the Father and the angels.
- For believers, this judgement is not meant to be terrifying but **deeply comforting**, because their full redemption will be completed and their cause will be publicly vindicated.
- Therefore Christians should **long for Christ’s return**, praying, “Come, Lord Jesus.”

So, the Belgic Confession presents the Last Judgement as the final public act of Christ’s justice: terrifying for the wicked, but joyful and comforting for believers.

questions.question: What do the Canons of Dort teach about divine predestination in Article 7?
questions.reference_answer:
Election is the unchangeable purpose of God, whereby, before the foundation of the world, He hath out of mere grace, according to the sovereign good pleasure of His own will, chosen, from the whole human race, which had fallen through their own fault from their primitive state of rectitude into sin and destruction, a certain number of persons to redemption in Christ, whom He from eternity appointed the Mediator and Head of the elect, and the foundation of salvation.

This elect number, though by nature neither better nor more deserving than others, but with them involved in one common misery, God hath decreed to give to Christ, to be saved by Him, and effectually to call and draw them to His communion by His Word and Spirit, to bestow upon them true faith, justification and sanctification; and having powerfully preserved them in the fellowship of His Son, finally, to glorify them for the demonstration of His mercy and for the praise of His glorious grace, as it is written: "According as He hath chosen us in Him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before Him in love: having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to Himself, according to the good pleasure of His will, to the praise of the glory of His grace, wherein He hath made us accepted in the beloved" (Eph. 1:4-6). And elsewhere: "Whom He did predestinate, them He also called: and whom He called, them He also justified: and whom He justified them He also glorified" (Rom. 8:30).

questions.question: What do the Canons of Dort teach about divine predestination in Article 9?
questions.reference_answer: This election was not founded upon foreseen faith, and the obedience of faith, holiness, or any other good quality or disposition in man, as the prerequisite, cause or condition on which it depended; but men are chosen to faith and to the obedience of faith, holiness, etc.; therefore election is the fountain of every saving good, from which proceeds faith, holiness, and the other gifts of salvation, and finally eternal life itself, as its fruits and effects, according to that of the apostle: "He hath chosen us [not because we were but] that we should be holy, and without blame, before Him in love" (Eph. 1:4).

questions.response:
In **Article 9 of the First Head of Doctrine** (“Election Not Based on Foreseen Faith”), the **Canons of Dort** teach that divine election is **not based on anything God foresees in a person**—not foreseen faith, obedience, holiness, or any other good quality.

Rather, God’s election is the **source** of these saving gifts. People are not chosen *because* they will believe or become holy; they are chosen *so that* they will receive faith, obedience, holiness, and ultimately eternal life.

In short: **predestination is unconditional**—grounded in God’s gracious will, not in foreseen human merit or response. Faith and holiness are the **fruits of election**, not its cause. The article appeals to Ephesians 1:4: God chose believers “that we should be holy and blameless before him.”

questions.response:
In the **Canons of Dort, Second Head of Doctrine, Article 1**—“The Death of Christ and the Redemption of Men Thereby”—the teaching is that:

- God is **supremely merciful**, but also **supremely just**.
- Because God is just, sin committed against His infinite majesty must be punished.
- That punishment is not only temporal, but also **eternal**, affecting both **body and soul**.
- Therefore, sinners cannot escape God’s judgment unless **satisfaction is made to God’s justice**.

In short, Article 1 teaches that human sin deserves eternal punishment, and redemption requires that God’s justice be satisfied—preparing the way for the teaching that Christ’s death provides that satisfaction.

questions.question: What do the Canons of Dort teach about the death of christ and the redemption of men in Article 8?
questions.reference_answer: For this was the sovereign counsel, and most gracious will and purpose of God the Father, that the quickening and saving efficacy of the most precious death of His Son should extend to all the elect, for bestowing upon them alone the gift of justifying faith, thereby to bring them infallibly to salvation: that is, it was the will of God, that Christ by the blood of the cross, whereby He confirmed the new covenant, should effectually redeem out of every people, tribe, nation, and language, all those, and those only, who were from eternity chosen to salvation and given to Him by the Father; that He should confer upon them faith, which together with all the other saving gifts of the Holy Spirit, He purchased for them by His death; should purge them from all sin, both original and actual, whether committed before or after believing; and having faithfully preserved them even to the end, should at last bring them free from every spot and blemish to the enjoyment of glory in His own presence forever.

questions.response:
In **Article 8 of the Second Head of Doctrine** (“The Death of Christ and the Redemption of Men”), the **Canons of Dort** teach that Christ’s death was intended by God to **effectually save the elect**.

In summary, Article 8 says:

- God’s gracious purpose was that the saving power of Christ’s death would extend to **all the elect**.
- Christ, by His blood, **effectually redeemed** people “out of every people, tribe, nation, and language.”
- He redeemed **all those, and only those**, whom the Father had chosen from eternity and given to Him.
- Christ’s death not only pays for sin but also **purchases faith** and all other saving gifts of the Holy Spirit for the elect.
- He cleanses them from **all sin**, both original and actual, whether committed before or after believing.
- He preserves them faithfully to the end and finally brings them into eternal glory.

So, Article 8 teaches what is often called **definite atonement** or **particular redemption**: Christ’s death is of infinite worth, but in God’s saving plan it is intended to actually redeem and secure the salvation of the elect.

questions.question: What do the Canons of Dort teach about the corruption of man and his conversion to god in Article 1?
questions.reference_answer: Man was originally formed after the image of God. His understanding was adorned with a true and saving knowledge of his Creator and of spiritual things; his heart and will were upright; all his affections pure; and the whole man was holy; but revolting from God by the instigation of the devil, and abusing the freedom of his own will, he forfeited these excellent gifts; and on the contrary entailed on himself blindness of mind, horrible darkness, vanity and perverseness of judgment, became wicked, rebellious, and obdurate in heart and will, and impure in his affections.

scoring.rubric: Must reflect the teaching of Canons of Dort, Head 3/4 (The Corruption of Man and His Conversion to God), Article 1. Should align with Reformed soteriology.

questions.response:
In **Canons of Dort, Third and Fourth Heads of Doctrine, Article 1**, the Synod teaches that:

- **Man was originally created in God’s image**—with true knowledge of God, righteousness, holiness, an upright will, and pure affections.
- **By the fall**, through the instigation of the devil and man’s own free will, humanity rebelled against God.
- As a result, man **lost those excellent gifts** and became corrupted:
  - blind in mind,
  - darkened in understanding,
  - vain and perverse in judgment,
  - wicked, rebellious, and hardened in heart and will,
  - impure in affections.

In short, Article 1 teaches that man was created holy and good, but through the fall he became deeply corrupted in every part of his nature, making conversion to God dependent on God’s gracious work.

questions.question: What do the Canons of Dort teach about the corruption of man and his conversion to god in Article 3?
questions.reference_answer: Therefore all men are conceived in sin, and by nature children of wrath, incapable of saving good, prone to evil, dead in sin, and in bondage thereto, and without the regenerating grace of the Holy Spirit, they are neither able nor willing to return to God, to reform the depravity of their nature, or to dispose themselves to reformation.

questions.response:
In the **Canons of Dort, Third and Fourth Heads of Doctrine, Article 3**—on “the corruption of man, his conversion to God, and the manner thereof”—the Synod teaches that fallen human beings are thoroughly corrupted by sin and cannot turn themselves back to God apart from grace.

In summary, Article 3 teaches:

- **All people are conceived in sin** and are by nature “children of wrath.”
- Humanity is **incapable of saving good** apart from grace.
- Fallen man is **inclined to evil**, “dead in sins,” and in bondage to sin.
- Therefore, a person **cannot by his own strength** return to God, reform his corrupt nature, or even prepare himself for such reform.
- Conversion requires the **regenerating grace of the Holy Spirit**.

A common English rendering says:

> “Therefore all men are conceived in sin, and are by nature children of wrath, incapable of saving good, prone to evil, dead in sin, and in bondage thereto; and without the regenerating grace of the Holy Spirit, they are neither able nor willing to return to God, to reform the depravity of their nature, nor to dispose themselves to reformation.”

So, Article 3 emphasizes the Reformed doctrine of **total depravity**: not that every person is as evil as possible, but that sin has corrupted every part of human nature, making divine grace absolutely necessary for true conversion to God.

questions.question: What do the Canons of Dort teach about the conversion of man and the manner thereof in Article 10?
questions.reference_answer: But that others who are called by the gospel obey the call and are converted is not to be ascribed to the proper exercise of free will, whereby one distinguishes himself above others, equally furnished with grace sufficient for faith and conversions as the proud heresy of Pelagius maintains; but it must be wholly ascribed to God, who as He has chosen His own from eternity in Christ, so He confers upon them faith and repentance, rescues them from the power of darkness, and translates them into the kingdom of His own Son, that they may show forth the praises of Him who hath called them out of darkness into His marvelous light; and may glory not in themselves, but in the Lord according to the testimony of the apostles in various places.

questions.response:
In the **Canons of Dort, Third and Fourth Heads of Doctrine, Article 10**, the Synod teaches that a person’s conversion is **not due to the exercise of human free will**, as though one person makes himself to differ from another who has the same grace offered. Rather, conversion is **wholly the work of God’s grace**.

Article 10 says that when some who are called by the gospel obey the call and are converted, this must be ascribed to God, who:

- chose his own in Christ from eternity,
- effectually calls them in time,
- gives them faith and repentance,
- delivers them from the power of darkness,
- brings them into the kingdom of his Son,

so that they may praise God and boast not in themselves, but in the Lord.

In short: **conversion is not ultimately caused by man’s free will, but by God’s sovereign, effectual grace.**

questions.question: What do the Canons of Dort teach about the conversion of man and the manner thereof in Article 11?
questions.reference_answer: But when God accomplishes His good pleasure in the elect or works in them true conversion, He not only causes the gospel to be externally preached to them and powerfully illuminates their mind by His Holy Spirit, that they may rightly understand and discern the things of the Spirit of God; but by the efficacy of the same regenerating Spirit, pervades the inmost recesses of the man; He opens the closed, and softens the hardened heart, and circumcises that which was uncircumcised, infuses new qualities into the will, which though heretofore dead, He quickens; from being evil, disobedient, and refractory, He renders it good, obedient, and pliable; actuates and strengthens it, that like a good tree, it may bring forth the fruits of good actions.

questions.response:
In the **Canons of Dort, Third and Fourth Heads of Doctrine, Article 11**, the Synod teaches that when God brings about the true conversion of His elect, He does more than have the gospel preached outwardly.

God converts a person by a powerful inward work of the Holy Spirit. Article 11 says that God:

- **causes the gospel to be preached outwardly**,  
- **powerfully enlightens the mind** by the Holy Spirit so that the person may understand and discern the things of God,  
- **penetrates the innermost being of man**,  
- **opens the closed heart**,  
- **softens the hard heart**,  
- **circumcises the uncircumcised heart**,  
- **infuses new qualities into the will**,  
- makes the will that was **dead alive**,  
- makes it **good instead of evil**,  
- makes it **willing instead of unwilling**,  
- makes it **obedient instead of stubborn**,  
- and strengthens the renewed will so that, like a good tree, it may produce good works.

In short, Article 11 teaches that conversion is not merely the result of external preaching or human persuasion. It is a **supernatural, inward, gracious work of God** by which He renews the mind, heart, and will, bringing the sinner willingly and truly to faith and obedience.

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about the holy scriptures?
questions.reference_answer: The Holy Scripture is the only sufficient, certain, and infallible rule of all saving Knowledge, Faith and Obedience; Although the light of Nature, and the works of Creation and Providence do so far manifest the goodness, wisdom and power of God, as to leave men unexcusable; yet are they not sufficient to give that knowledge of God and His will, which is necessary unto Salvation. Therefore it pleased the Lord at sundry times, and in divers manners, to reveal himself, and to declare that His will unto his Church; and afterward for the better preserving, and propagating of the Truth, and for the more sure Establishment, and Comfort of the Church against the corruption of the flesh, and the malice of Satan, and of the World, to commit the same wholly unto writing; which maketh the Holy Scriptures to be most necessary, those former ways of Gods revealing his will unto his people being now ceased. Under the Name of Holy Scripture or the Word of God written; are now contained all the Books of the Old and New Testament which are these: Of the Old Testament: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, The Song of Songs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi. Of the New Testament: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, The Acts of the Apostles, Pauls Epistle to the Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Phillippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, to Titus, to Philemon, the Epistle to the Hebrews, the Epistle of James, the First and Second Epistles of Peter, the First, Second and Third Epistles of John, the Epistle of Jude, the Revelation. The Books commonly called Apocrypha not being of Divine inspiration, are no part of the Canon (or rule) of the Scripture, and therefore are of no authority to the Church of God, nor to be any otherwise approved or made use of, then other humane writings. The Authority of the Holy Scripture for which it ought to be believed dependeth not upon the testimony of any man, or Church; but wholly upon God (who is truth it self) the Author thereof; therefore it is to be received, because it is the Word of God. We may be moved and induced by the testimony of the Church of God, to an high and reverent esteem of the Holy Scriptures; and the heavenliness of the matter, the efficacy of the Doctrine, and the Majesty of the stile, the consent of all the parts, the scope of the whole (which is to give all glory to God) the full discovery it makes of the only way of mans salvation, and many other incomparable Excellencies, and intire perfections thereof, are arguments whereby it doth abundantly evidence it self to be the Word of God; yet notwithstanding; our full perswasion, and assurance of the infallible truth, and divine authority thereof, is from the inward work of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness by and with the Word in our Hearts. The whole Councel of God concerning all things necessary for his own Glory, Mans Salvation, Faith and Life, is either expressely set down or necessarily contained in the Holy Scripture; unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new Revelation of the Spirit, or traditions of men.Nevertheless we acknowledge the inward illumination of the Spirit of God, to be necessary for the saving understanding of such things as are revealed in the Word, and that there are some circumstances concerning the worship of God, and government of the Church common to humane actions and societies; which are to be ordered by the light of nature, and Christian prudence according to the general rules of the Word, which are always to be observed. All things in Scripture are not alike plain in themselves, nor alike clear unto all; yet those things which are necessary to be known, believed, and observed for Salvation, are so clearly propounded, and opened in some place of Scripture or other, that not only the learned, but the unlearned, in a due use of ordinary means, may attain to a sufficient understanding of them. The Old Testament in Hebrew, (which was the Native language of the people of God of old) and the New Testament in Greek (which at the time of the writing of it was most generally known to the Nations being immediately inspired by God, and by his singular care and Providence kept pure in all Ages, are therefore authentical; so as in all controversies of Religion the Church is finally to appeal unto them But because these original tongues are not known to all the people of God, who have a right unto, and interest in the Scriptures, and are commanded in the fear of God to read and search them, therefore they are to be translated into the vulgar language of every Nation, unto which they come, that the Word of God dwelling plentifully in all, they may worship him in an acceptable manner, and through patience and comfort of the Scriptures may have hope. The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture it self: And therefore when there is a question about the true and full sense of any Scripture (which is not manifold but one) it must be searched by other places that speak more clearly. The supream judge by which all controversies of Religion are to be determined, and all Decrees of Councels, opinions of antient Writers, Doctrines of men, and private Spirits, are to be examined, and in whose sentence we are to rest, can be no other but the Holy Scripture delivered by the Spirit, into which Scripture so delivered, our faith is finally resolved.

scoring.rubric: Must address the key points of Chapter 1 (Of the Holy Scriptures). Should align with the 1689 London Baptist Confession's Reformed Baptist theology.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith**, in **Chapter 1: “Of the Holy Scriptures,”** teaches that Scripture is the final, sufficient, and authoritative written revelation of God. In summary, it says:

1. **Scripture is necessary for salvation**  
   Creation and providence reveal God’s power, wisdom, and goodness enough to leave people without excuse, but they are not sufficient to give saving knowledge of God. Therefore, God gave His Word in writing for the church’s preservation, comfort, and instruction.

2. **The Bible consists of the 66 canonical books**  
   The Confession lists the books of the Old and New Testaments and identifies them as the Word of God. It rejects the Apocrypha as inspired Scripture, saying those books have no more authority in the church than other human writings.

3. **Scripture’s authority comes from God, not the church**  
   The Bible is to be believed and obeyed because it is the Word of God. Its authority does not depend on the testimony of any person or church.

4. **The Holy Spirit convinces believers of Scripture’s truth**  
   The church may testify to Scripture’s value, and Scripture itself shows many evidences of divine origin. But full assurance that it is God’s Word comes from the inward work of the Holy Spirit.

5. **Scripture is sufficient**  
   Everything necessary for God’s glory, human salvation, faith, and obedience is either expressly stated in Scripture or necessarily contained in it. No new revelations or human traditions are needed as additions to Scripture.

6. **Some matters require wisdom and prudence**  
   The Confession recognizes that certain circumstances of worship and church order are not spelled out in detail, but are to be ordered by the light of nature and Christian wisdom according to Scripture’s general rules.

7. **Scripture is clear in what is necessary for salvation**  
   Not every passage is equally plain, and not everyone understands Scripture equally well. Yet the essential truths necessary for salvation are clear enough that both learned and ordinary believers can understand them through the proper use of ordinary means.

8. **Scripture was originally given in Hebrew and Greek**  
   The Old Testament in Hebrew and the New Testament in Greek are the authentic texts. Because all God’s people have a right to the Scriptures, they should be translated into the common languages of the nations.

9. **Scripture interprets Scripture**  
   The infallible rule for interpreting Scripture is Scripture itself. Therefore, unclear passages should be understood in light of clearer passages.

10. **Scripture is the supreme judge in all religious controversies**  
   Councils, ancient writers, human opinions, and private spirits are not the final authority. The final judge is “the Holy Scripture delivered by the Spirit,” or the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture.

In short, the 1689 Confession teaches that **the Bible alone is God’s inspired, authoritative, sufficient, clear, preserved, translatable, and final rule for faith and life.**

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about god and of the holy trinity?
questions.reference_answer: The Lord our God is but one only living, and true God; whose subsistence is in and of himself, infinite in being, and perfection, whose Essence cannot be comprehended by any but himself; a most pure spirit, invisible, without body, parts, or passions, who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light, which no man can approach unto, who is immutable, immense, eternal, incomprehensible, Almighty, every way infinit, most holy, most wise, most free, most absolute, working all things according to the councel of his own immutable, and most righteous will, for his own glory, most loving, gracious, merciful, long suffering, abundant in goodness and truth, forgiving iniquity, transgression and sin, the rewarder of them that diligently seek him, and withall most just, and terrible in his judgements, hating all sin, and who will by no means clear the guilty. God having all life, glory, goodness, blessedness, in and of himself: is alone in, and unto himself all-sufficient, not standing in need of any Creature which he hath made, nor deriving any glory from them, but onely manifesting his own glory in, by, unto, and upon them, he is the alone fountain of all Being, of whom, through whom, and to whom are all things, and he hath most soveraign dominion over all creatures, to do by them, for them, or upon them, whatsoever himself pleaseth; in his sight all things are open and manifest, his knowledge is infinite, infallible, and independant upon the Creature, so as nothing is to him contingent, or uncertain; he is most holy in all his Councels, in all his Works, and in all his Commands; to him is due from Angels and men, whatsoever worship, service, or obedience as Creatures they owe unto the Creator, and whatever he is further pleased to require of them. In this divine and infinite Being there are three subsistences, the Father the Word (or Son) and Holy Spirit, of one substance, power, and Eternity, each having the whole Divine Essence, yet the Essence undivided, the Father is of none neither begotten nor proceeding, the Son is Eternally begotten of the Father, the holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son, all infinite, without beginning, therefore but one God, who is not to be divided in nature and Being; but distinguished by several peculiar, relative properties, and personal relations; which doctrine of the Trinity is the foundation of all our Communion with God, and comfortable dependance on him.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession**, Chapter 2, **“Of God and of the Holy Trinity,”** teaches historic orthodox Christian doctrine about God and the Trinity.

### 1. There is one true God

It begins by confessing that:

> “The Lord our God is but one only living and true God.”

God is the only God, living and true, and He exists eternally in and of Himself. He is not dependent on creation for anything.

### 2. God’s nature and attributes

The confession teaches that God is:

- **Infinite in being and perfection**
- **A pure spirit**
- **Invisible**
- **Without body, parts, or passions**
- **Immutable** — unchanging
- **Immense** — not limited by space
- **Eternal**
- **Incomprehensible** — beyond full human understanding
- **Almighty**
- **Most wise**
- **Most holy**
- **Most free**
- **Most absolute**

God does all things according to the counsel of His own will and for His own glory.

The confession also emphasizes God’s moral perfection. He is:

- Loving
- Gracious
- Merciful
- Longsuffering
- Abundant in goodness and truth
- Forgiving of iniquity, transgression, and sin

But He also:

- Hates sin
- Is perfectly just
- Will not clear the guilty apart from justice

### 3. God is self-sufficient and sovereign

The confession teaches that God has all life, glory, goodness, and blessedness **in and of Himself**. He does not need His creatures, nor does He gain anything from them.

Yet He is the source of all things and has sovereign dominion over all creation. Nothing is hidden from Him; His knowledge is infinite, infallible, and independent of the creature.

### 4. God is Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit

The confession then teaches that within the one divine Being there are three distinct “subsistences,” or persons:

- **The Father**
- **The Word or Son**
- **The Holy Spirit**

These three are not three gods, but one God. Each person is fully and truly God, sharing the same divine essence.

The confession says:

> “In this divine and infinite Being there are three subsistences, the Father, the Word or Son, and Holy Spirit, of one substance, power, and eternity.”

### 5. The persons are distinguished by their personal relations

The confession distinguishes the three persons in this way:

- **The Father** is of none — neither begotten nor proceeding.
- **The Son** is eternally begotten of the Father.
- **The Holy Spirit** proceeds from the Father and the Son.

This reflects classic Nicene Trinitarian theology.

### 6. The Trinity is foundational to Christian faith

The confession says the doctrine of the Trinity is the foundation of all our communion with God and our comfort in depending upon Him.

In short, the 1689 London Baptist Confession teaches that there is **one living and true God**, perfect in all His attributes, sovereign over all things, and that this one God eternally exists as **Father, Son, and Holy Spirit** — three distinct persons, one divine essence.

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about god's decree?
questions.reference_answer: God hath Decreed in himself from all Eternity, by the most wise and holy Councel of his own will, freely and unchangeably, all things whatsoever comes to passe; yet so as thereby is God neither the author of sin, nor hath fellowship with any therein, nor is violence offered to the will of the Creature, nor yet is the liberty, or contingency of second causes taken away, but rather established, in which appears his wisdom in disposing all things, and power, and faithfulness in accomplishing his Decree. Although God knoweth whatsoever may, or can come to passe upon all supposed conditions; yet hath he not Decreed anything, because he foresaw it as future, or as that which would come to pass upon such conditions. By the decree of God for the manifestation of his glory some men and Angels, are predestinated, or fore-ordained to Eternal Life, through Jesus Christ to the praise of his glorious grace; others being left to act in their sin to their just condemnation, to the praise of his glorious justice. These Angels and Men thus predestinated, and fore-ordained, are particularly, and unchangeably designed; and their number so certain, and definite, that it cannot be either increased, or diminished. Those of mankind that are predestinated to life, God before the foundation of the world was laid, according to his eternal and immutable purpose, and the secret Councel and good pleasure of his will, hath chosen in Christ unto everlasting glory, out of his meer free grace and love; without any other thing in the creature as a condition or cause moving him thereunto. As God hath appointed the Elect unto glory, so he hath by the eternal and most free purpose of his will, fore-ordained all the means thereunto, wherefore they who are elected, being faln in Adam, are redeemed by Christ, are effectually called unto faith in Christ, by his spirit working in due season, are justifyed, adopted, sanctified, and kept by his power through faith unto salvation; neither are any other redeemed by Christ, or effectually called, justified, adopted, sanctified, and saved, but the Elect only. The Doctrine of this high mystery of predestination, is to be handled with special prudence, and care; that men attending the will of God revealed in his word, and yeilding obedience thereunto, may from the certainty of their effectual vocation, be assured of their eternal election; so shall this doctrine afford matter of praise, reverence, and admiration of God, and of humility, diligence, and abundant consolation, to all that sincerely obey the Gospel.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith**, chapter 3, “Of God’s Decree,” teaches that God has an eternal, sovereign, wise, and holy plan for everything that happens.

In summary, it teaches:

1. **God decreed all things from eternity**  
   God “freely and unchangeably” ordained whatsoever comes to pass, according to the wise and holy counsel of His will.

2. **God is not the author of sin**  
   Although all things fall under God’s decree, the confession carefully denies that God is the author of sin or that He has fellowship with evil.

3. **Human responsibility and secondary causes are real**  
   God’s decree does not violate the will of creatures or destroy ordinary causes and choices. Rather, God’s decree establishes them. This is a compatibilist view: God is sovereign, and humans remain responsible.

4. **God’s decree is not based on foreseen events**  
   God knows all possible outcomes, but He did not decree things because He foresaw they would happen. His decree comes from His own will and purpose, not from foreseen human faith, works, or decisions.

5. **God predestines some angels and people to eternal life**  
   For the manifestation of His glory, God chose some to eternal life in Christ, “to the praise of his glorious grace.”

6. **Others are passed by and left to their sin**  
   The confession says others are “left to act in their sin” and come under just condemnation, “to the praise of his glorious justice.” It presents condemnation as just punishment for sin, not as God committing evil.

7. **The elect are chosen particularly and unchangeably**  
   The number of the elect is fixed and cannot be increased or diminished.

8. **Election is entirely of free grace**  
   Those chosen to life were chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world, not because of anything foreseen in them, but solely because of God’s free grace and love.

9. **God ordains both the end and the means**  
   God not only appoints the elect to glory, but also ordains the means: redemption by Christ, effectual calling, faith, justification, adoption, sanctification, and perseverance.

10. **The doctrine should be handled carefully and pastorally**  
   The confession says this “high mystery” should be treated with prudence and care. Properly understood, it should lead to praise, reverence, humility, diligence, assurance, and comfort for believers.

In short, the 1689 Confession teaches a strongly Reformed doctrine of God’s decree: **God sovereignly ordains all things for His glory, elects sinners to salvation by grace in Christ, leaves others to just condemnation for their sin, and yet remains holy, while human responsibility remains real.**

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about divine providence?
questions.reference_answer: God the good Creator of all things, in his infinite power, and wisdom, doth uphold, direct, dispose, and govern all Creatures, and things, from the greatest even to the least, by his most wise and holy providence, to the end for the which they were Created; according unto his infallible foreknowledge, and the free and immutable Councel of his own will; to the praise of the glory of his wisdom, power, justice, infinite goodness and mercy. Although in relation to the foreknowledge and Decree of God, the first cause, all things come to pass immutably and infallibly; so that there is not any thing, befalls any by chance, or without his Providence; yet by the same Providence he ordereth them to fall out, according to the nature of second causes, either necessarily, freely, or contingently. God in his ordinary Providence maketh use of means; yet is free to work, without, above, and against them at his pleasure. The Almighty power, unsearchable wisdom, and infinite goodness of God, so far manifest themselves in his Providence, that his determinate Councel extendeth it self even to the first fall, and all other sinful actions both of Angels, and Men; (and that not by a bare permission) which also he most wisely and powerfully boundeth, and otherwise ordereth, and governeth, in a manifold dispensation to his most holy ends: yet so, as the sinfulness of their acts proceedeth only from the Creatures, and not from God; who being most holy and righteous, neither is nor can be, the author or approver of sin. The most wise, righteous, and gracious God, doth oftentimes, leave for a season his own children to manifold temptations, and the corruptions of their own heart, to chastise them for their former sins, or to discover unto them the hidden strength of corruption, and deceitfulness of their hearts, that they may be humbled; and to raise them to a more close, and constant dependence for their support, upon himself; and to make them more watchful against all future occasions of sin, and for other just and holy ends. As for those wicked and ungodly men, whom God as a righteous judge, for former sin doth blind and harden; from them he not only withholdeth his Grace, whereby they might have been inlightned in their understanding, and wrought upon in their hearts: But sometimes also withdraweth the gifts which they had, and exposeth them to such objects as their corruptions makes occasion of sin; and withall gives them over to their own lusts, the temptations of the world, and the power of Satan, whereby it comes to pass, that they harden themselves, even under those means which God useth for the softning of others. As the Providence of God doth in general reach to all Creatures, so after a most special manner it taketh care of his Church, and disposeth of all things to the good thereof.

scoring.rubric: Must address the key points of Chapter 5 (Of Divine Providence). Should align with the 1689 London Baptist Confession's Reformed Baptist theology.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith**, in **Chapter 5, “Of Divine Providence,”** teaches that God sovereignly governs all things in creation according to his wisdom, power, goodness, and holy will.

In summary, it says:

1. **God upholds and governs everything**  
   God, as the good Creator, “upholdeth, directeth, disposeth, and governeth” all creatures and events, from the greatest to the least, according to his foreknowledge and unchangeable will, for his own glory.

2. **Nothing happens by chance**  
   All things come to pass under God’s providence. Yet God ordinarily works through “second causes,” meaning created means and real creaturely actions. Events may occur necessarily, freely, or contingently, but never outside God’s rule.

3. **God uses means, but is not bound by them**  
   In ordinary providence God works through means—such as natural processes, human decisions, and ordinary circumstances. But he is free to work **without**, **above**, or **against** those means whenever he pleases.

4. **God’s providence extends even over sin, without making God the author of sin**  
   The Confession says God’s providence extends even to the fall and to sinful actions of angels and men. However, God is not the author or approver of sin. The sinfulness belongs to the creature, while God wisely and holily orders even sinful acts to accomplish his purposes.

5. **God uses trials for the good of his people**  
   God may allow his children to face temptations, inward corruption, and hardships in order to humble them, discipline them, expose their weakness, increase their dependence on him, and make them watchful. Whatever happens to the elect is appointed for God’s glory and their good.

6. **God may judicially harden the wicked**  
   As a righteous judge, God may blind or harden the ungodly because of their sin. He may withhold grace, withdraw gifts, expose them to occasions of sin, and give them over to their own lusts, the world, and Satan.

7. **God has special care for his church**  
   While God’s providence extends over all creation, he governs all things in a special way for the good of his church.

In short, the 1689 Confession teaches an **exhaustive, wise, holy, and purposeful providence**: God rules over all things, nothing is accidental, human choices remain real, evil is never attributable to God as sin, and all things are ultimately directed to God’s glory and the good of his people.

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about god's covenant?
questions.reference_answer: The distance between God and the Creature is so great, that although reasonable Creatures do owe obedience unto him as their Creator, yet they could never have attained the reward of Life, but by some voluntary condescension on Gods part, which he hath been pleased to express, by way of Covenant. Moreover Man having brought himself under the curse of the Law by his fall, it pleased the Lord to make a Covenant of Grace wherein he freely offereth unto Sinners, Life and Salvation by Jesus Christ, requiring of them Faith in him, that they may be saved; and promising to give unto all those that are ordained unto eternal Life, his holy Spirit, to make them willing, and able to believe. This Covenant is revealed in the Gospel; first of all to Adam in the promise of Salvation by the seed of the woman, and afterwards by farther steps, untill the full discovery thereof was compleated in the new Testament; and it is founded in that Eternal Covenant transaction, that was between the Father and the Son, about the Redemption of the Elect; and it is alone by the Grace of this Covenant, that all of the posterity of fallen Adam, that ever were saved, did obtain life and a blessed immortality; Man being now utterly uncapable of acceptance with God upon those terms, on which Adam stood in his state of innocency.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** teaches about God’s covenant mainly in **Chapter 7, “Of God’s Covenant.”** In summary:

1. **God relates to humanity by covenant because of his voluntary condescension.**  
   God is infinitely above his creatures. Though humans owe him obedience as Creator, they could never attain blessedness or the “reward of life” unless God freely chose to enter into covenant with them.

2. **After the fall, God made a covenant of grace.**  
   Humanity fell under the curse of the law through Adam’s sin. Therefore, God was pleased to make a **covenant of grace**, in which he freely offers sinners life and salvation through **Jesus Christ**.

3. **The covenant of grace requires faith in Christ.**  
   Salvation in this covenant is received by faith in Christ, not by human merit or obedience to the law.

4. **God promises the Holy Spirit to the elect.**  
   The confession says God promises to give his Holy Spirit to all those ordained to eternal life, making them willing and able to believe.

5. **The covenant of grace was revealed progressively.**  
   It was first revealed to Adam in the promise that the seed of the woman would crush the serpent, then revealed more fully through the history of redemption, and finally made fully known in the New Testament.

6. **The covenant is grounded in an eternal covenant of redemption.**  
   The confession says the covenant of grace is founded in an eternal covenant transaction between the Father and the Son concerning the redemption of the elect.

7. **All salvation after the fall is by this covenant alone.**  
   No one is saved by the “law of innocency” or by works. All the saved, from Adam onward, are saved by grace through Christ.

So, in simple terms, the 1689 Confession teaches that **God graciously covenants to save fallen sinners through Jesus Christ, that this salvation is received by faith, applied by the Holy Spirit, progressively revealed in Scripture, and rooted in God’s eternal plan to redeem his elect.**

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about christ the mediator?
questions.reference_answer: It pleased God in his eternal purpose, to chuse and ordain the Lord Jesus his only begotten Son, according to the Covenant made between them both, to be the Mediator between God and Man; the Prophet, Priest and King; Head and Saviour of his Church, the heir of all things, and judge of the world: Unto whom he did from all Eternity give a people to be his seed, and to be by him in time redeemed, called, justified, sanctified, and glorified. The Son of God, the second Person in the Holy Trinity, being very and eternal God, the brightness of the Fathers glory, of one substance and equal with him: who made the World, who upholdeth and governeth all things he hath made: did when the fullness of time was come take unto him mans nature, with all the Essential properties, and common infirmities thereof, yet without sin: being conceived by the Holy Spirit in the Womb of the Virgin Mary, the Holy Spirit coming down upon her, and the power of the most High overshadowing her, and so was made of a Woman, of the Tribe of Judah, of the Seed of Abraham, and David according to the Scriptures: So that two whole, perfect, and distinct natures, were inseparably joined together in one Person: without conversion, composition, or confusion: which Person is very God, and very Man; yet one Christ, the only Mediator between God and Man. The Lord Jesus in his humane nature thus united to the divine, in the Person of the Son, was sanctified, and anointed with the Holy Spirit, above measure; having in him all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; in whom it pleased the Father that all fullness should dwell: To the end that being holy, harmless, undefiled, and full of Grace, and Truth, he might be throughly furnished to execute the office of a Mediator, and Surety; which office he took not upon himself, but was thereunto called by his Father; who also put all power and judgement in his hand, and gave him Commandement to execute the same. This office the Lord Jesus did most willingly undertake, which that he might discharge he was made under the Law, and did perfectly fulfill it, and underwent the punishment due to us, which we should have born and suffered, being made Sin and a Curse for us: enduring most grievous sorrows in his Soul; and most painful sufferings in his body; was crucified, and died, and remained in the state of the dead; yet saw no corruption: on the third day he arose from the dead, with the same body in which he suffered; with which he also ascended into heaven: and there sitteth at the right hand of his Father, making intercession; and shall return to judge Men and Angels, at the end of the World. The Lord Jesus by his perfect obedience and sacrifice of himself, which he through the Eternal Spirit once offered up unto God, hath fully satisfied the Justice of God, procured reconciliation, and purchased an Everlasting inheritance in the Kingdom of Heaven, for all those whom the Father hath given unto him. Although the price of Redemption was not actually paid by Christ, till after his Incarnation, yet the vertue, efficacy, and benefit thereof were communicated to the Elect in all ages successively, from the beginning of the World, in and by those Promises, Types, and Sacrifices, wherein he was revealed, and signified to be the Seed of the Woman, which should bruise the Serpents head; and the Lamb slain from the foundation of the World: Being the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever. Christ in the work of Mediation acteth according to both natures, by each nature doing that which is proper to it self; yet by reason of the Unity of the Person, that which is proper to one nature, is sometimes in Scripture attributed to the Person denominated by the other nature. To all those for whom Christ hath obtained eternal redemption, he doth certainly, and effectually apply, and communicate the same; making intercession for them, uniting them to himself by his spirit, revealing unto them, in and by the word, the mystery of salvation; perswading them to believe, and obey; governing their hearts by his word and spirit, and overcoming all their enemies by his Almighty power, and wisdom; in such manner, and wayes as are most consonant to his wonderful, and unsearchable dispensation; and all of free, and absolute Grace, without any condition foreseen in them, to procure it. This office of Mediator between God and Man, is proper onely to Christ, who is the Prophet, Priest, and King of the Church of God; and may not be either in whole, or any part thereof transfer'd from him to any other. This number and order of Offices is necessary; for in respect of our ignorance, we stand in need of his prophetical Office; and in respect of our alienation from God, and imperfection of the best of our services, we need his Priestly office, to reconcile us, and present us acceptable unto God: and in respect our averseness, and utter inability to return to God, and for our rescue, and security from our spiritual adversaries, we need his Kingly office, to convince, subdue, draw, uphold, deliver, and preserve us to his Heavenly Kingdome.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession**, chapter 8, “**Of Christ the Mediator**,” teaches that Jesus Christ is the only Mediator between God and humanity, appointed by God from eternity to redeem His people. In summary, it teaches:

1. **Christ was eternally appointed as Mediator**  
   God chose and ordained His Son, according to the eternal covenant, to be the Mediator between God and man. Christ is the **Prophet, Priest, and King**, the Head and Savior of the church, Heir of all things, and Judge of the world.

2. **Christ has two natures in one person**  
   Jesus is truly God and truly man. The eternal Son of God took on a real human nature, being conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary. His divine and human natures are united in one person “without conversion, composition, or confusion.”

3. **Christ was fully equipped for His mediatorial office**  
   The Father anointed Him with the Holy Spirit beyond measure and gave Him all authority and judgment, so that He might perfectly accomplish salvation.

4. **Christ willingly accomplished redemption**  
   Jesus voluntarily took on the office of Mediator. He was born under the law, perfectly obeyed it, suffered the punishment due for sin, was crucified, died, was buried, rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, intercedes for His people, and will return to judge the world.

5. **Christ’s sacrifice fully satisfied God’s justice**  
   By His perfect obedience and once-for-all sacrifice, Christ fully satisfied divine justice, reconciled His people to God, and secured for them an everlasting inheritance.

6. **Christ’s work saves believers in all ages**  
   Though Christ’s redemption was accomplished in history through His incarnation, death, and resurrection, its saving benefits were applied to the elect even before His coming, through promises, types, and sacrifices.

7. **Christ acts according to both natures**  
   In His mediatorial work, Christ acts as both God and man, each nature doing what is proper to it, yet always as one person.

8. **Christ effectually applies salvation to His people**  
   Those for whom Christ obtained redemption are certainly brought to receive its benefits. He intercedes for them, unites them to Himself by the Spirit, reveals salvation through the Word, gives faith and obedience, governs their hearts, and overcomes their enemies.

9. **Christ alone is Mediator**  
   The office of Mediator belongs only to Christ. No one else may share or replace His role as Prophet, Priest, or King of the church.

10. **His threefold office meets humanity’s need**  
   Because we are ignorant, we need Christ as **Prophet** to reveal God’s truth. Because we are guilty and alienated from God, we need Him as **Priest** to reconcile us by sacrifice and intercession. Because we are weak, rebellious, and under spiritual enemies, we need Him as **King** to rule, defend, and preserve us.

In short, the 1689 Confession teaches that **Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God made man, is the only and all-sufficient Mediator who accomplishes and applies salvation to His people as Prophet, Priest, and King.**

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about effectual calling?
questions.reference_answer: Those whom God hath predestinated unto Life, he is pleased in his appointed, and accepted time, effectually to call by his word, and Spirit, out of that state of sin, and death, in which they are by nature, to grace and Salvation by Jesus Christ; inlightning their minds, spiritually, and savingly to understand the things of God; taking away their heart of stone, and giving unto them an heart of flesh; renewing their wills, and by his Almighty power determining them to that which is good, and effectually drawing them to Jesus Christ; yet so as they come most freely, being made willing by his Grace. This Effectual Call is of God's free, and special grace alone, not from any thing at all foreseen in man, nor from any power, or agency in the Creature, coworking with his special Grace, the Creature being wholly passive therein, being dead in sins and trespasses, until being quickned & renewed by the holy Spirit, he is thereby enabled to answer this call, and to embrace the Grace offered and conveyed in it; and that by no less power, then that which raised up Christ from the dead. Elect Infants dying in infancy, are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit; who worketh when, and where, and how he pleaseth: so also are all other elect persons, who are uncapable of being outwardly called by the Ministry of the Word. Others not elected, although they may be called by the Ministry of the word, and may have some common operations of the Spirit, yet not being effectually drawn by the Father, they neither will, nor can truly come to Christ; and therefore cannot be saved: much less can men that receive not the Christian Religion be saved; be they never so diligent to frame their lives according to the light of nature, and the Law of that Religion they do profess.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession**, chapter 10, “Of Effectual Calling,” teaches that effectual calling is God’s sovereign, gracious work by which he brings his elect to salvation in Christ.

In summary:

1. **God effectually calls all whom he has predestined to life**  
   At God’s appointed time, he calls them “by his Word and Spirit” out of their natural state of sin and death into grace and salvation through Jesus Christ.

2. **This call changes the whole person**  
   God enlightens the mind to understand spiritual truth, removes the “heart of stone,” gives a “heart of flesh,” renews the will, and draws the sinner to Christ. Yet the person comes **freely**, because God’s grace makes them willing.

3. **It is entirely of God’s free grace**  
   Effectual calling is not based on anything God foresees in the person, nor on human cooperation prior to grace. Since sinners are “dead in sins and trespasses,” they are passive until the Holy Spirit makes them alive and enables them to respond.

4. **It is distinct from the outward gospel call**  
   Some people hear the Word externally and may experience “common operations of the Spirit,” but unless they are effectually drawn by the Father, they will not and cannot truly come to Christ.

5. **Elect infants and others incapable of outward calling are saved by Christ through the Spirit**  
   The confession says elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works “when, and where, and how he pleaseth.” The same applies to elect persons incapable of being outwardly called by the ministry of the Word.

So, the 1689 Confession teaches that effectual calling is **monergistic**—God alone brings it about. It is the inward, saving call of the Holy Spirit that makes the outward gospel call effective, bringing the elect willingly and certainly to Christ.

questions.response:
The **1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith** teaches that **justification** is God’s gracious, legal declaration that sinners are righteous in his sight **solely because of Christ**, received **through faith alone**. Its main teaching is found in **Chapter 11, “Of Justification.”**

Key points:

1. **Justification is an act of God’s free grace**  
   God justifies those whom he effectually calls. He does this by **pardoning their sins** and **counting them righteous**, not by making them inherently righteous as the basis of acceptance.

2. **It is not based on anything in the believer**  
   The Confession denies that justification is grounded in works, faith considered as a meritorious act, or any “evangelical obedience.” Faith is not the righteousness itself; it is the means by which the believer receives Christ.

3. **Christ’s righteousness is imputed to believers**  
   Believers are justified because God credits to them Christ’s righteousness—his **active obedience** to God’s law and his **passive obedience** in suffering and death. Christ’s obedience and satisfaction are the believer’s “whole and sole righteousness.”

4. **Faith alone is the instrument of justification**  
   The Confession says faith “receiving and resting on Christ and his righteousness” is the **alone instrument** of justification. Yet this faith is never alone in the justified person; it is always accompanied by saving graces and “works by love.”

5. **Justification is fully grounded in Christ’s atonement**  
   Christ, by his obedience and death, fully satisfied God’s justice for all who are justified. Therefore, justification displays both God’s **justice** and his **free grace**.

6. **God decreed justification eternally, but applies it in time**  
   God decreed from eternity to justify the elect, and Christ died and rose for their justification. Nevertheless, individuals are not personally justified until the Holy Spirit actually applies Christ to them.

7. **The justified remain justified, though they may fall under fatherly displeasure**  
   Believers can never fall from the state of justification, but through sin they may lose the sense of God’s favor until they humble themselves, confess, repent, and renew faith.

8. **Old Testament and New Testament believers are justified the same way**  
   The Confession teaches that believers before Christ and after Christ are justified in the same way: by grace, through faith, on the basis of Christ.

In short, the 1689 teaches a classic Reformed Baptist doctrine of justification: **by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, based on the imputed righteousness of Christ alone, to the glory of God alone.**

In summary, it teaches:

1. **True believers will never totally or finally fall away from grace.**

2. **Their perseverance rests on God, not on their own strength.**

4. **Such sins have real consequences.**  
   When believers fall, they may displease God, grieve the Holy Spirit, lose comfort and assurance, wound their consciences, scandalize others, and bring temporal judgments upon themselves.

5. **Yet God will preserve and restore them.**  
   Though they may fall seriously, they will not be finally lost. God will renew them to repentance and preserve them by his power unto salvation.

A key line from the confession is that true believers:

> “can neither totally nor finally fall from the state of grace, but shall certainly persevere therein to the end, and be eternally saved.”

So, the 1689 Confession teaches a robust Reformed Baptist view: **all true saints will persevere because God preserves them**, though they may experience real struggles, sins, and seasons of spiritual darkness along the way.

questions.response:
In historic Christian theology, the short answer is:

**Fallen man cannot choose God savingly by his own unaided free will; he must first be acted upon by God’s grace.**

Because of the Fall, human beings still make real choices, but their wills are morally bound by sin. Apart from grace, man does not naturally desire God or submit to Him.

Key texts often cited:

- **John 6:44** — “No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him.”
- **Romans 8:7–8** — “The mind set on the flesh is hostile to God… those who are in the flesh cannot please God.”
- **1 Corinthians 2:14** — “The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God…”
- **Ephesians 2:1–5** — Man is “dead in trespasses and sins,” but God makes him alive.
- **Philippians 2:13** — “It is God who works in you, both to will and to work for His good pleasure.”

Different traditions explain this differently:

- **Reformed/Augustinian view:** Fallen man is unable to choose God until God regenerates him and gives him a new heart.
- **Arminian/Wesleyan view:** Fallen man cannot choose God unaided, but God gives prevenient grace that enables a genuine response.
- **Catholic/Orthodox view:** God’s grace must come first, but man can cooperate with that grace.

So if by “free will” you mean **natural human ability apart from grace**, then **no**.  
If you mean **a real human response enabled by God’s grace**, then **yes**, man truly chooses—but only because God first draws, awakens, and enables him.

questions.response:
It depends on what you mean by **“spiritually good.”**

### If you mean: *Can an unregenerate person do outwardly good or moral things?*  
**Yes.** Unbelievers can love family, give to the poor, act justly, tell the truth, and benefit society. Christians often call this **civil good** or the fruit of **common grace**.

### If you mean: *Can an unregenerate person do something truly pleasing to God in the saving/spiritual sense—flowing from faith, love for God, and aiming at His glory?*  
**No, not apart from grace.** Scripture says:

- “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” — **Romans 8:8**
- “Without faith it is impossible to please Him” — **Hebrews 11:6**
- “Whatever does not proceed from faith is sin” — **Romans 14:23**
- “There is none who seeks for God” — **Romans 3:11**

So in the Augustinian/Reformed sense, an unregenerate person may do deeds that are outwardly good, but they are not **spiritually good before God** because they do not arise from a renewed heart, true faith, or love for God’s glory.

### Important distinction  
Their good actions may be genuinely helpful and morally better than evil actions, but they do not merit salvation or make the person righteous before God. Only faith in Christ, produced by God’s grace, makes a person acceptable before Him.

So the short answer is:

**An unregenerate person can do outwardly good things, but not spiritually good things that are pleasing to God in the fullest saving sense, unless God’s grace first works in them.**

questions.question: Does the fall affect every part of human nature?
questions.reference_answer: The fall corrupted every faculty of man Mind, will, and affections are all affected This is total depravity — not utter depravity

questions.response:
Yes—within historic Christian theology, the fall is generally understood to affect every part of human nature: mind, will, desires, emotions, body, and relationships.

This is often called **total depravity** or **radical corruption**, especially in Reformed theology. It does **not** mean that every person is as evil as possible, or that humans are incapable of any outward good. Rather, it means that sin’s effects extend to the whole person:

- **Mind**: our understanding is darkened and distorted by sin.  
- **Will**: our choices are bent away from God.  
- **Desires/Affections**: we love lesser things wrongly or more than God.  
- **Body**: we are subject to suffering, decay, and death.  
- **Relationships**: alienation from God, others, creation, and even ourselves.  

However, Christianity also teaches that the **image of God remains** in humanity after the fall. Human nature is deeply wounded and corrupted, but not destroyed. People still have dignity, moral awareness, rationality, and the capacity for real though imperfect good.

So the short answer is: **yes, the fall affects every part of human nature, but it does not erase the image of God or make human beings worthless.**

questions.question: Does God choose to save people based on foreseen faith?
questions.reference_answer: Election is not based on foreseen faith or merit Election is according to God's sovereign good pleasure Faith is the result, not the cause, of election

required_points: Election is not based on foreseen faith or merit
Election is according to God's sovereign good pleasure
Faith is the result, not the cause, of election

questions.response:
Christians disagree on this, especially between **Arminian/Wesleyan** and **Reformed/Calvinist** traditions.

## 1. Arminian/Wesleyan answer: **Yes, in a qualified sense**
God elects people “according to foreknowledge” — meaning he chooses to save those whom he foreknows will respond to his grace with faith.

Key texts often cited:

- **Romans 8:29** — “those whom he foreknew he also predestined”
- **1 Peter 1:1–2** — elect “according to the foreknowledge of God”
- **John 3:16** — “whoever believes”
- **1 Timothy 2:4** — God “desires all people to be saved”

In this view, God’s choice is not arbitrary. He foresees who will freely believe, aided by grace, and elects them in Christ. Faith is the condition of salvation, but not a meritorious work.

## 2. Reformed/Calvinist answer: **No**
God does not choose people because he foresees their faith. Rather, he chooses them by his sovereign grace, and their faith is the result of that election.

Key texts often cited:

- **Ephesians 1:4–5** — God chose us “before the foundation of the world”
- **Romans 9:11–16** — election is “not because of works but because of him who calls”
- **John 6:37, 44** — those given by the Father come to Christ
- **Acts 13:48** — “as many as were appointed to eternal life believed”

In this view, “foreknowledge” means more than God foreseeing facts; it means God setting his covenant love on someone beforehand. So faith is not the basis of election but the gift that flows from election.

## 3. A concise comparison

| View | Does God elect based on foreseen faith? |
|---|---|
| Arminian/Wesleyan | Yes, God foreknows who will believe |
| Reformed/Calvinist | No, God gives faith because he elected |
| Catholic/Orthodox | Often emphasize mystery, grace, free response, and God’s foreknowledge without reducing salvation to either human merit or strict determinism |

## Bottom line

If you mean, “Does God save people through faith?” — **yes**, all orthodox Christians affirm that.

If you mean, “Is foreseen faith the reason God elected certain people?” — **Arminians generally say yes; Calvinists generally say no.**

questions.question: Is God's election of individuals to salvation conditional or unconditional?
questions.reference_answer: Election is unconditional It is based solely on God's sovereign will No human merit or action conditions God's choice

required_points: Election is unconditional
It is based solely on God's sovereign will
No human merit or action conditions God's choice

questions.response:
Christians disagree on this, and the answer depends on one’s theological tradition.

## 1. Unconditional election  
In **Augustinian/Reformed/Calvinist** theology, God’s election of individuals to salvation is **unconditional**.

That means God chose certain people for salvation **not because of foreseen faith, works, merit, or any condition in them**, but solely according to His sovereign grace and purpose.

Commonly cited passages include:

- **Ephesians 1:4–5** — “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world… according to the purpose of his will.”
- **Romans 9:11–16** — “not because of works but because of him who calls… it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy.”
- **2 Timothy 1:9** — God saved us “not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace.”

In this view, faith itself is a gift resulting from election, not the condition God foresaw in order to elect.

## 2. Conditional election  
In **Arminian/Wesleyan** theology, election is usually understood as **conditional**.

That means God elects people **in view of their faith in Christ**. God foreknows who will freely respond to His grace and believe, and He elects them accordingly.

Commonly cited passages include:

- **Romans 8:29** — “those whom he foreknew he also predestined.”
- **1 Peter 1:1–2** — “elect according to the foreknowledge of God.”
- **John 3:16** — “whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.”
- **1 Timothy 2:4** — God “desires all people to be saved.”

In this view, salvation is still by grace, but election is conditioned on faith, not on human merit.

## 3. Other views  
Some traditions emphasize **corporate election**: God elects Christ as the chosen one, and individuals share in election by being united to Christ through faith. This view is often connected to passages like:

- **Ephesians 1:4** — “He chose us in him.”

## Summary  
So the main answers are:

- **Reformed/Calvinist:** Election is **unconditional**.  
- **Arminian/Wesleyan:** Election is **conditional on faith**.  
- **Corporate election view:** God elects a people “in Christ,” and individuals participate through union with Him.

If asking from a specifically Reformed perspective, the answer is: **God’s election of individuals to salvation is unconditional, based solely on His gracious will, not on foreseen faith or works.**

In Scripture, the atonement is presented as effective and accomplishing what God intended:

- “You shall call his name Jesus, for **he will save his people from their sins**.” — Matthew 1:21  
- “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd **lays down his life for the sheep**.” — John 10:11

That said, the gospel is to be preached sincerely to all people, and everyone who believes in Christ will be saved. The common Reformed way of saying it is:

> Christ’s death is **sufficient for all**, but **efficient for the elect**.

So the answer is: **Christ died to truly and effectually save His people; He did not merely make salvation possible.**

questions.response:
Yes—this is a classic way many Reformed theologians summarize the atonement:

**Christ’s atonement is sufficient for all, but efficient only for the elect.**

Meaning:

- **Sufficient for all:** Because Christ is the infinite Son of God, His sacrifice has infinite worth and is fully able to save every human being if God so willed. There is no lack in the value or power of Christ’s death.
- **Efficient only for the elect:** In God’s saving purpose, the benefits of Christ’s atonement are actually applied only to those whom God has chosen and brings to faith by the Holy Spirit.

So the statement distinguishes between the **intrinsic worth** of Christ’s death and its **saving application**.

A common Reformed formulation is:

> Christ’s death is sufficient for the whole world, but intended by God to effectively redeem the elect.

This is tied to the doctrine often called **limited atonement** or **definite atonement**—not meaning Christ’s death is limited in value, but that it is definite in its saving intent and effect.

However, different Christian traditions understand this differently:

- **Reformed/Calvinist:** Sufficient for all, efficient for the elect.
- **Arminian/Wesleyan:** Christ died for all equally, but only believers benefit.
- **Lutheran:** Christ atoned for all, though only believers receive the benefit.
- **Amyraldian/“hypothetical universalist”:** Christ died for all in some sense, but God elects some to receive the benefits.

So, within classic Reformed theology, the answer is: **Yes.**

questions.response:
In classic **Reformed/Calvinist theology**, the answer is **no**: those whom God has chosen to save cannot **ultimately** resist His saving grace.

They may resist God for a time, reject the gospel outwardly, and struggle with sin, but God’s grace toward the elect is understood to be **effectual**—it actually brings them to faith and keeps them to the end.

Key texts often cited include:

- **John 6:37** — “All that the Father gives me will come to me…”
- **John 6:44** — “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him…”
- **Romans 8:30** — “Those whom he predestined he also called… justified… glorified.”
- **Philippians 1:6** — God “will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.”

This doctrine is often called **irresistible grace** or, more precisely, **effectual calling**. It does not mean God drags people to salvation against their will. Rather, God changes the heart so that the person comes willingly to Christ.

However, other Christian traditions answer differently. **Arminian/Wesleyan** theology, for example, teaches that God’s grace enables salvation but can be resisted even by those genuinely called. Some traditions also distinguish between God’s eternal election and a person’s ongoing cooperation with grace.

So, in short:

- **Reformed view:** No, the elect cannot ultimately resist God’s saving grace.  
- **Arminian/Wesleyan view:** Yes, grace can be resisted.  
- **Catholic/Orthodox views:** Grace is necessary, but human cooperation remains significant.

If you are asking from the standpoint of Calvinist doctrine, the answer is: **God’s chosen people may resist for a time, but they will not finally overcome His saving grace.**
