questions.question: What Scripture passages teach the doctrine of original sin?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 5:12, Rom 5:18-19, Ps 51:5, Gen 3:6-7
questions.response:
The phrase **“original sin”** is not itself in Scripture, but the doctrine is drawn from several passages that teach that humanity’s sinfulness is rooted in Adam’s fall and that people are sinful from birth/nature.

## Key passages

### 1. **Genesis 3**
The fall of Adam and Eve is the foundation: sin enters human experience through their disobedience, bringing shame, alienation from God, death, and curse.

> “You shall not eat of it… lest you die.” — Genesis 3:3  
> “To dust you shall return.” — Genesis 3:19

### 2. **Romans 5:12–21**
This is the central New Testament passage for original sin. Paul connects Adam’s sin with the sin and death of all humanity, and contrasts Adam with Christ.

> “Sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned.” — Romans 5:12  
> “By the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners.” — Romans 5:19

### 3. **1 Corinthians 15:21–22**
Paul again links Adam with death and Christ with resurrection.

> “For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.”

### 4. **Psalm 51:5**
David speaks of sinfulness from conception or birth.

> “Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me.”

### 5. **Psalm 58:3**
This passage describes wickedness as present from the earliest stage of life.

> “The wicked are estranged from the womb; they go astray from birth, speaking lies.”

### 6. **Ephesians 2:1–3**
Paul describes people as spiritually dead and “by nature” under wrath before salvation.

> “You were dead in the trespasses and sins…” — Ephesians 2:1  
> “and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind.” — Ephesians 2:3

### 7. **John 3:5–6**
Jesus teaches that natural birth is insufficient; fallen human nature requires spiritual rebirth.

> “That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.”

### 8. **Genesis 6:5 and Genesis 8:21**
These passages emphasize the deep corruption of the human heart.

> “Every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.” — Genesis 6:5  
> “The intention of man’s heart is evil from his youth.” — Genesis 8:21

### 9. **Romans 3:9–23**
Paul teaches the universal sinfulness of Jews and Gentiles alike.

> “None is righteous, no, not one.” — Romans 3:10  
> “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23

## Summary

The doctrine of original sin is especially grounded in:

- **Genesis 3** — Adam and Eve’s fall  
- **Romans 5:12–21** — Adam’s sin affects all humanity  
- **Psalm 51:5** — sinfulness from conception/birth  
- **Ephesians 2:1–3** — humanity is spiritually dead and “by nature” under wrath  
- **1 Corinthians 15:21–22** — in Adam all die; in Christ life comes

Different Christian traditions explain the details differently—especially whether Adam’s guilt is imputed to his descendants or whether humanity inherits corruption and death—but these are the main biblical texts used to support the doctrine.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach the doctrine of the Trinity?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 28:19, 2 Cor 13:14, John 1:1, Gen 1:26
questions.response:
The word **“Trinity”** is not used in the Bible, but Christians say the doctrine is taught by the Bible as a whole through three main claims:

1. **There is one God**
2. **The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are each spoken of as God**
3. **The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are personally distinct**

## 1. The Bible teaches there is one God

- **Deuteronomy 6:4** — “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one.”
- **Isaiah 45:5** — “I am the LORD, and there is no other, besides me there is no God.”
- **1 Timothy 2:5** — “There is one God…”

Christian Trinitarianism does not teach three gods, but one God.

## 2. The Father is God

This is widely assumed throughout Scripture.

- **John 6:27** — Jesus refers to “God the Father.”
- **1 Corinthians 8:6** — “For us there is one God, the Father…”
- **Ephesians 4:6** — “One God and Father of all…”

## 3. The Son is God

Several passages identify Jesus with deity.

- **John 1:1** — “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”
- **John 1:14** — “The Word became flesh…”
- **John 20:28** — Thomas says to Jesus, “My Lord and my God!”
- **Colossians 2:9** — “In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily.”
- **Hebrews 1:8** — Of the Son: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.”
- **Titus 2:13** — “Our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.”

Jesus also does things Scripture associates with God, such as forgiving sins, receiving worship, creating, judging, and giving eternal life.

## 4. The Holy Spirit is God

The Holy Spirit is not merely an impersonal force; he speaks, teaches, guides, can be grieved, and is identified with God.

- **Acts 5:3–4** — Peter says Ananias lied to the Holy Spirit, then says, “You have not lied to man but to God.”
- **1 Corinthians 3:16** — “You are God’s temple and… God’s Spirit dwells in you.”
- **2 Corinthians 3:17** — “Now the Lord is the Spirit…”
- **Ephesians 4:30** — “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God.”

## 5. The Father, Son, and Spirit are distinct

The Bible does not simply say that Father, Son, and Spirit are three names for the same person. They relate to one another.

- **Matthew 3:16–17** — At Jesus’ baptism, the Son is baptized, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks from heaven.
- **John 14:16–17** — Jesus says he will ask the Father, and the Father will give “another Helper,” the Spirit.
- **John 17:1–5** — Jesus prays to the Father and speaks of glory he had with the Father before the world existed.
- **Romans 8:26–34** — The Spirit intercedes, Christ intercedes, and God is addressed distinctly.

## 6. The three are named together

Some passages place Father, Son, and Spirit together in a way that became central for Trinitarian doctrine.

- **Matthew 28:19** — “Baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”
- **2 Corinthians 13:14** — “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.”
- **1 Peter 1:2** — Believers are chosen according to the Father’s foreknowledge, sanctified by the Spirit, for obedience to Jesus Christ.
- **Ephesians 4:4–6** — “One Spirit… one Lord… one God and Father…”

## In summary

The doctrine of the Trinity is the Christian attempt to hold together everything the Bible teaches:

- **There is one God.**
- **The Father is God.**
- **The Son is God.**
- **The Holy Spirit is God.**
- **The Father, Son, and Spirit are distinct from one another.**

So, while the Bible does not contain the later technical formula “one essence, three persons,” Trinitarian Christians believe that formula summarizes the biblical teaching.

questions.question: What passages affirm the full deity of Jesus Christ?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: John 1:1, John 1:14, Col 2:9, Heb 1:3, Phil 2:6
questions.response:
Here are key biblical passages commonly cited to affirm the full deity of Jesus Christ:

## Direct statements that Jesus is God

- **John 1:1, 14** — “The Word was God… And the Word became flesh.”  
  Jesus is identified as the eternal Word who is God and who became incarnate.

- **John 20:28** — Thomas says to Jesus, “My Lord and my God!”  
  Jesus receives this confession without rebuke.

- **Romans 9:5** — Christ is described as “God over all, blessed forever.”  

- **Titus 2:13** — “Our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.”  

- **2 Peter 1:1** — “Our God and Savior Jesus Christ.”  

- **Hebrews 1:8** — Of the Son it says, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.”

- **1 John 5:20** — Jesus Christ is called “the true God and eternal life.”

## Passages affirming the fullness of deity in Christ

- **Colossians 2:9** — “In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily.”

- **Colossians 1:15–19** — Christ is the image of the invisible God; all things were created through him and for him; “in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell.”

- **Philippians 2:5–11** — Christ existed “in the form of God,” humbled himself, and is exalted so that every knee bows to him.

## Jesus shares divine names, glory, and honors

- **John 8:58** — Jesus says, “Before Abraham was, I am.”  
  This echoes the divine self-identification in **Exodus 3:14**.

- **John 17:5** — Jesus speaks of the glory he had with the Father “before the world existed.”

- **Revelation 1:17–18** — Jesus says, “I am the first and the last,” a title used of God in Isaiah.

- **Revelation 22:13** — “I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.”

## Jesus does works only God does

- **John 1:3** — “All things were made through him.”  
  Jesus is presented as Creator, not a created being.

- **Hebrews 1:2–3** — Through the Son God made the world; the Son is “the radiance of the glory of God” and “the exact imprint of his nature.”

- **Hebrews 1:10–12** — The Son is addressed with words from Psalm 102 about Yahweh as Creator.

- **Mark 2:5–12** — Jesus forgives sins, prompting the question, “Who can forgive sins but God alone?”

## Jesus receives worship

- **Matthew 14:33** — The disciples worship Jesus and say, “Truly you are the Son of God.”

- **Matthew 28:9, 17** — The risen Jesus is worshiped by his disciples.

- **John 9:38** — The healed man says, “Lord, I believe,” and worships Jesus.

- **Hebrews 1:6** — “Let all God’s angels worship him.”

- **Revelation 5:11–14** — The Lamb receives worship alongside the One seated on the throne.

## Old Testament Yahweh texts applied to Jesus

- **Isaiah 40:3 / Mark 1:2–3** — The way prepared for Yahweh is applied to Jesus.

- **Joel 2:32 / Romans 10:9–13** — Calling on the name of the Lord, originally Yahweh, is applied to Jesus.

- **Isaiah 45:23 / Philippians 2:10–11** — Every knee bowing to Yahweh is applied to Jesus.

- **Psalm 102:25–27 / Hebrews 1:10–12** — A psalm about Yahweh as eternal Creator is applied to the Son.

In summary, the strongest passages include **John 1:1–14, John 20:28, Colossians 2:9, Hebrews 1:8, Titus 2:13, 2 Peter 1:1, Philippians 2:5–11, and Revelation 5:11–14**.

questions.question: Which Bible passages teach the bodily resurrection of Christ?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Cor 15:3-8, Matt 28:5-6, Luke 24:39, John 20:27
questions.response:
The Bible teaches Christ’s **bodily resurrection** in many places—especially by emphasizing the **empty tomb**, His **physical wounds**, His ability to be **touched**, and His eating with the disciples after rising.

## Key Gospel passages

- **Matthew 28:5–9** — The angel says Jesus “has risen,” and the women take hold of His feet.
- **Mark 16:1–8** — The tomb is empty: “He has risen; he is not here.”
- **Luke 24:36–43** — Jesus explicitly denies being a spirit:  
  > “See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.”  
  He also eats fish in their presence.
- **John 2:19–22** — Jesus predicts the resurrection of “the temple of his body.”
- **John 20:19–29** — Jesus shows His hands and side; Thomas is invited to touch His wounds.
- **John 21:9–14** — The risen Jesus eats with His disciples by the Sea of Galilee.

## Acts

- **Acts 1:3** — Jesus presents Himself alive “by many proofs” over forty days.
- **Acts 2:24–32** — Peter says Jesus was raised and that His “flesh” did not see corruption, quoting Psalm 16.
- **Acts 10:40–41** — Peter says the risen Jesus appeared to witnesses “who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.”
- **Acts 13:29–37** — Paul teaches that Jesus was raised and did not undergo decay.

## Paul’s letters

- **Romans 6:4–10** — Christ was raised from the dead and dies no more.
- **Romans 8:11** — God raised Jesus from the dead and will also give life to believers’ mortal bodies.
- **1 Corinthians 15:3–8** — Paul summarizes the gospel: Christ died, was buried, was raised, and appeared to many witnesses.
- **1 Corinthians 15:12–20** — Paul insists that Christ’s resurrection is essential to the faith.
- **1 Corinthians 15:35–49** — Paul discusses the resurrection body, with Christ as the pattern.
- **Philippians 3:20–21** — Christ will transform believers’ lowly bodies to be like His glorious body.
- **Colossians 2:12** — Believers are raised with Christ through faith.

## Other New Testament passages

- **1 Peter 1:3** — God gave believers new birth “through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.”
- **1 Peter 3:18** — Christ was “put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit.”
- **Revelation 1:17–18** — The risen Jesus says, “I died, and behold I am alive forevermore.”

A few of the clearest passages for the **bodily** nature of the resurrection are **Luke 24:39–43**, **John 20:27**, **John 2:19–22**, **Acts 2:31**, and **Acts 10:40–41**.

questions.question: What Scripture supports the doctrine of substitutionary atonement?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Isa 53:5-6, 2 Cor 5:21, 1 Pet 2:24, Rom 3:25
questions.response:
The doctrine of **substitutionary atonement** teaches that Christ died **for sinners**, bearing sin, judgment, and the curse in their place, so that they might be forgiven and reconciled to God.

Here are major Scriptures commonly used to support it:

## 1. Isaiah 53 — The Suffering Servant bears others’ sins

Isaiah 53 is one of the clearest Old Testament passages.

> “He was pierced for our transgressions;  
> he was crushed for our iniquities;  
> upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace,  
> and with his wounds we are healed.”  
> — **Isaiah 53:5**

> “The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.”  
> — **Isaiah 53:6**

> “He shall bear their iniquities.”  
> — **Isaiah 53:11**

> “He bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors.”  
> — **Isaiah 53:12**

This passage presents the Servant suffering not merely as an example, but **on behalf of others** and **bearing their iniquities**.

## 2. Jesus gives His life as a ransom

> “The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”  
> — **Mark 10:45**

Also:

> “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.”  
> — **Matthew 26:28**

Jesus describes His death as being “for many” and connected directly to the forgiveness of sins.

## 3. Christ died “for” the ungodly and sinners

> “While we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.”  
> — **Romans 5:6**

> “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”  
> — **Romans 5:8**

> “While we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son.”  
> — **Romans 5:10**

Paul presents Christ’s death as an act done **for us** while we were sinners and enemies of God.

## 4. Christ was made sin for us

> “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.”  
> — **2 Corinthians 5:21**

This is a central substitutionary text: the sinless Christ is identified with sin “for our sake,” so that believers receive righteousness in Him.

## 5. Christ bore the curse of the law

> “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree.’”  
> — **Galatians 3:13**

Here Christ takes the curse associated with sin and law-breaking “for us.”

## 6. Christ died for our sins

> “Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures.”  
> — **1 Corinthians 15:3**

This is part of Paul’s summary of the gospel. Christ’s death is specifically “for our sins,” not merely as a martyr or moral example.

## 7. Christ bore our sins in His body

> “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed.”  
> — **1 Peter 2:24**

Peter directly applies Isaiah 53 to Jesus and says He “bore our sins.”

## 8. Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous

> “For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God.”  
> — **1 Peter 3:18**

This verse clearly presents substitution: **the righteous** suffers for **the unrighteous**.

## 9. Hebrews: Christ offered Himself as a sacrifice for sins

> “He has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.”  
> — **Hebrews 9:26**

> “Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many…”  
> — **Hebrews 9:28**

> “We have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.”  
> — **Hebrews 10:10**

Hebrews connects Christ’s death to the Old Testament sacrificial system, portraying Him as both priest and sacrifice.

## 10. Old Testament sacrificial background

The sacrificial system prepared the way for substitutionary language.

> “He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him.”  
> — **Leviticus 1:4**

> “The priest shall make atonement for him for the sin which he has committed, and he shall be forgiven.”  
> — **Leviticus 4:35**

The animal sacrifice symbolically stands in the place of the worshiper, making atonement for sin.

## 11. The Passover lamb

> “When I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague will befall you to destroy you.”  
> — **Exodus 12:13**

The New Testament connects Christ to the Passover lamb:

> “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.”  
> — **1 Corinthians 5:7**

The Passover imagery supports the idea of deliverance through the death of another.

## 12. Christ as the propitiation for sin

> “Whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith.”  
> — **Romans 3:25**

> “He is the propitiation for our sins.”  
> — **1 John 2:2**

> “God… sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.”  
> — **1 John 4:10**

“Propitiation” refers to a sacrifice that turns away wrath and deals with sin before God.

---

In summary, the doctrine of substitutionary atonement is supported especially by passages such as **Isaiah 53**, **Mark 10:45**, **Romans 5:6–10**, **2 Corinthians 5:21**, **Galatians 3:13**, **1 Peter 2:24**, **1 Peter 3:18**, and **Hebrews 9–10**. These texts teach that Christ died **for us**, **bore our sins**, **became a curse for us**, and suffered **the righteous for the unrighteous** to bring sinners to God.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach the imputation of Christ's righteousness?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 2 Cor 5:21, Rom 4:3-6, Phil 3:9, Rom 5:19
questions.response:
The Bible does not use the exact phrase **“imputation of Christ’s righteousness,”** but the doctrine is commonly drawn from several passages where righteousness is described as being **counted, credited, reckoned, or received** by faith rather than earned by works.

## Key passages

### 1. **2 Corinthians 5:21**
> “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.”

This is one of the clearest texts. Christ, who was sinless, is treated as sin for us; believers, “in him,” become righteous before God. Many theologians see here a double exchange: our sin counted to Christ, and his righteousness counted to us.

---

### 2. **Romans 4:3–8**
> “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.”  
> “And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness…”

Paul repeatedly uses the language of **counting** or **reckoning** righteousness. He cites Abraham and David to show that justification is not based on works but on righteousness credited by faith.

---

### 3. **Philippians 3:8–9**
> “…not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith.”

Paul contrasts two kinds of righteousness: his own law-based righteousness versus a righteousness from God received through faith in Christ.

---

### 4. **Romans 5:18–19**
> “As one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men.  
> For as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous.”

Paul compares Adam and Christ. Adam’s sin brings condemnation to those united to him; Christ’s obedience brings righteousness and justification to those united to him. This is a major text for the idea that Christ’s obedience counts for his people.

---

### 5. **1 Corinthians 1:30**
> “And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption.”

Christ himself is said to be our “righteousness.” Believers are righteous because they are united to Christ.

---

### 6. **Jeremiah 23:5–6**
> “And this is the name by which he will be called: ‘The LORD is our righteousness.’”

This messianic prophecy is often understood as anticipating that God’s people will have righteousness in and through the coming Davidic King.

---

### 7. **Isaiah 53:11**
> “By his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities.”

The suffering servant bears the sins of others and makes many righteous. This is closely connected to substitution and justification.

---

## Summary

The doctrine is especially taught in:

- **2 Corinthians 5:21** — Christ made sin for us; we become righteousness in him.  
- **Romans 4** — righteousness is counted/credited by faith.  
- **Philippians 3:9** — believers have righteousness from God, not their own.  
- **Romans 5:18–19** — Christ’s obedience makes many righteous.  
- **1 Corinthians 1:30** — Christ is our righteousness.

In short, the Bible teaches that sinners are justified not by their own righteousness, but by a righteousness from God received through faith, grounded in union with Christ and his obedient work.

questions.question: What passages describe the process of sanctification?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Thess 4:3, Phil 2:12-13, 2 Cor 3:18, Heb 12:14
questions.response:
Here are key Bible passages that describe the process of sanctification—God making believers holy and conforming them to Christ.

## Core passages on sanctification

### 1. **1 Thessalonians 4:3–8**
> “For this is the will of God, your sanctification…”  
Paul connects sanctification with holiness in conduct, especially sexual purity and self-control.

### 2. **1 Thessalonians 5:23–24**
> “Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely…”  
Sanctification is presented as God’s work, affecting the whole person—spirit, soul, and body.

### 3. **John 17:17**
> “Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.”  
Jesus teaches that sanctification happens through God’s truth, especially His Word.

### 4. **2 Corinthians 3:18**
> “We… are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another.”  
This describes sanctification as a gradual transformation into Christlikeness by the Spirit.

### 5. **Romans 6:19–22**
> “Present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification…”  
Paul describes sanctification as a new pattern of life after being freed from sin.

### 6. **Romans 12:1–2**
> “Be transformed by the renewal of your mind…”  
Sanctification involves offering oneself to God and being inwardly renewed rather than conformed to the world.

### 7. **Galatians 5:16–25**
> “Walk by the Spirit…”  
This passage contrasts the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit, showing sanctification as Spirit-led living.

### 8. **Ephesians 4:20–24**
> “Put off your old self… be renewed… put on the new self…”  
Sanctification includes rejecting the old sinful way of life and putting on the new life created after God’s likeness.

### 9. **Colossians 3:1–17**
> “Put to death therefore what is earthly in you…”  
Paul describes sanctification as putting sin to death and putting on compassion, humility, forgiveness, love, and thankfulness.

### 10. **Philippians 2:12–13**
> “Work out your own salvation… for it is God who works in you…”  
Sanctification involves both human responsibility and God’s empowering work.

## Other important passages

### 11. **Hebrews 12:10–14**
> “He disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness.”  
God uses discipline and hardship to produce holiness.

### 12. **Titus 2:11–14**
> “The grace of God… trains us to renounce ungodliness…”  
Grace not only forgives but also trains believers to live godly lives.

### 13. **1 Peter 1:14–16**
> “Be holy in all your conduct…”  
Believers are called to holiness because God Himself is holy.

### 14. **2 Peter 1:3–8**
> “Make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue…”  
Sanctification is described as growth in godly qualities.

### 15. **1 John 3:2–3**
> “Everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself…”  
The hope of seeing Christ motivates purity now.

## Summary

The process of sanctification is described as:

- **God’s work in believers** — 1 Thessalonians 5:23; Philippians 2:13  
- **Transformation by the Spirit** — 2 Corinthians 3:18; Galatians 5:16–25  
- **Renewal through the Word and truth** — John 17:17; Romans 12:2  
- **Putting off sin and putting on righteousness** — Ephesians 4:20–24; Colossians 3:1–17  
- **Growing in holiness over time** — 2 Peter 1:3–8; Hebrews 12:10–14  
- **Becoming more like Christ** — Romans 8:29; 2 Corinthians 3:18

questions.question: Where does Scripture teach about the means of grace?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 10:17, Acts 2:42, 1 Cor 11:23-26, Matt 28:19
questions.response:
Scripture teaches the doctrine of the **means of grace** even though the exact phrase “means of grace” is not itself a biblical phrase. The idea is that God ordinarily gives, strengthens, and nourishes faith through appointed means—especially **the Word, the sacraments, and prayer**.

### 1. A summary text: Acts 2:42

> “And they devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.”  
> — **Acts 2:42**

This verse is often seen as a compact picture of the church’s ordinary life of grace: **the Word** “apostles’ teaching,” **the Lord’s Supper** “breaking of bread,” **prayer**, and the fellowship of the church.

### 2. The Word as a means of grace

Scripture teaches that God creates and strengthens faith through his Word.

> “So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.”  
> — **Romans 10:17**

> “Receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.”  
> — **James 1:21**

> “Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk, that by it you may grow up into salvation.”  
> — **1 Peter 2:2**

> “Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.”  
> — **John 17:17**

> “The sacred writings… are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.”  
> — **2 Timothy 3:15–17**

### 3. Baptism as a means of grace

Baptism is given by Christ and joined in Scripture to union with Christ, forgiveness, and incorporation into the visible church.

> “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them…”  
> — **Matthew 28:19**

> “Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins…”  
> — **Acts 2:38–39**

> “All of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death.”  
> — **Romans 6:3–4**

> “For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.”  
> — **Galatians 3:27**

### 4. The Lord’s Supper as a means of grace

The Lord’s Supper is not merely a memorial; Scripture speaks of it as a real participation or communion in Christ.

> “The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ?”  
> — **1 Corinthians 10:16**

> “This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me… This cup is the new covenant in my blood.”  
> — **1 Corinthians 11:23–26**

> “They devoted themselves… to the breaking of bread…”  
> — **Acts 2:42**

### 5. Prayer as a means of grace

God commands prayer and promises to hear and bless his people through it.

> “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.”  
> — **Matthew 7:7**

> “How much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!”  
> — **Luke 11:13**

> “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.”  
> — **Hebrews 4:16**

> “Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God.”  
> — **Philippians 4:6–7**

### In summary

The clearest biblical pattern is found in **Acts 2:42**: the church receives grace through devotion to **the apostles’ teaching, the breaking of bread, and the prayers**. Other passages explain how God uses these means: the **Word** creates and nourishes faith, **baptism** and the **Lord’s Supper** signify and seal Christ’s benefits, and **prayer** brings believers to the throne of grace.

questions.question: What Bible passages support covenant theology?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gen 17:7, Jer 31:31-34, Heb 8:6-13, Gal 3:29
questions.response:
Covenant theology is supported by a broad biblical pattern: God relates to humanity through covenants, and the various biblical covenants unfold one unified plan of redemption fulfilled in Christ.

Below are major passages often used to support covenant theology.

## 1. God’s covenantal relationship with Adam

Though the word “covenant” is not used in Genesis 2, covenant theologians argue that the elements of a covenant are present: God gives Adam a command, promises life, warns of death, and Adam acts as representative head of humanity.

- **Genesis 2:15–17** — Adam is commanded not to eat from the tree; death is threatened for disobedience.
- **Genesis 3:15** — The first gospel promise: the seed of the woman will crush the serpent.
- **Romans 5:12–21** — Adam and Christ are compared as representative heads; Adam brings condemnation, Christ brings righteousness and life.
- **1 Corinthians 15:21–22, 45–49** — Adam and Christ are contrasted as the first man and the last Adam.
- **Hosea 6:7** — “Like Adam they transgressed the covenant” is often cited as evidence that Adam’s relationship with God was covenantal.

This is often called the **covenant of works** or **covenant of creation**.

## 2. The covenant of grace promised after the fall

Covenant theology teaches that after Adam’s fall, God saves sinners by grace through faith in the promised Redeemer.

- **Genesis 3:15** — The promise of victory through the woman’s seed.
- **Genesis 12:1–3** — God promises Abraham land, offspring, blessing, and that all nations will be blessed through him.
- **Genesis 15:1–6** — Abraham believes God, and it is counted to him as righteousness.
- **Genesis 17:1–14** — God establishes his covenant with Abraham and his offspring.
- **Romans 4:1–25** — Paul uses Abraham as the model of justification by faith.
- **Galatians 3:6–29** — The Abrahamic promise is fulfilled in Christ, and believers are Abraham’s offspring by faith.

## 3. Unity of the Old and New Testaments

Covenant theology emphasizes that there is one saving plan throughout Scripture, centered on Christ.

- **Luke 24:25–27, 44–47** — Jesus teaches that the Law, Prophets, and Psalms point to him.
- **John 5:39, 46** — The Scriptures testify about Christ; Moses wrote of him.
- **Acts 2:39** — Peter says the promise is “for you and for your children and for all who are far off.”
- **Acts 3:24–26** — The prophets proclaimed the days of Christ, and the Abrahamic promise is applied to the gospel.
- **Romans 15:8–12** — Christ confirms the promises to the patriarchs and brings Gentiles into praise.
- **Ephesians 2:11–22** — Gentiles who were strangers to the covenants are brought near in Christ and made one people with Jewish believers.

## 4. The Abrahamic covenant fulfilled in Christ

The New Testament strongly connects the Abrahamic covenant to Christ and the gospel.

- **Genesis 12:3** — “In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.”
- **Galatians 3:8** — Scripture “preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham.”
- **Galatians 3:16** — The promised “offspring” is ultimately Christ.
- **Galatians 3:29** — Those who belong to Christ are Abraham’s offspring and heirs according to promise.
- **Romans 4:11–17** — Abraham is the father of all who believe, circumcised and uncircumcised.

These passages are central for the covenant-theology view that the church is not a separate plan from Israel, but the fulfillment and expansion of God’s covenant people in Christ.

## 5. The Mosaic covenant within God’s gracious plan

Covenant theology usually sees the Mosaic covenant as part of the covenant of grace, though with a distinct legal/national administration for Israel.

- **Exodus 19:4–6** — God calls Israel his treasured possession, kingdom of priests, and holy nation.
- **Exodus 24:3–8** — The covenant is ratified with blood.
- **Leviticus 18:5** — “The person who does them shall live by them.”
- **Deuteronomy 7:6–9** — God chose Israel because of his covenant love, not because of their greatness.
- **Deuteronomy 30:1–10** — God promises future heart renewal and restoration.
- **Galatians 3:17–24** — The law, given after Abraham, does not annul the promise; it served as a guardian until Christ.
- **Romans 10:4** — Christ is the end/goal of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

## 6. The Davidic covenant and Christ’s kingship

The Davidic covenant promises a king whose throne will be established forever, fulfilled in Jesus Christ.

- **2 Samuel 7:12–16** — God promises David an everlasting throne.
- **Psalm 89:3–4, 34–37** — God swears covenant faithfulness to David.
- **Isaiah 9:6–7** — The promised Son will reign on David’s throne forever.
- **Luke 1:31–33** — Jesus receives the throne of his father David and reigns forever.
- **Acts 2:29–36** — Peter says Christ’s resurrection and exaltation fulfill the Davidic promise.
- **Romans 1:1–4** — Jesus is descended from David and declared Son of God in power.

## 7. The New Covenant promised and fulfilled

Covenant theology sees the New Covenant as the fulfillment of the previous covenants, not a completely unrelated plan.

- **Jeremiah 31:31–34** — God promises a new covenant with forgiveness of sins and the law written on the heart.
- **Ezekiel 36:25–27** — God promises cleansing, a new heart, and the Spirit.
- **Luke 22:20** — Jesus says, “This cup…is the new covenant in my blood.”
- **1 Corinthians 11:25** — Paul repeats the institution of the Lord’s Supper as the new covenant in Christ’s blood.
- **2 Corinthians 3:6–18** — Paul contrasts the old covenant ministry with the new covenant ministry of the Spirit.
- **Hebrews 8:6–13** — Christ mediates a better covenant, fulfilling Jeremiah’s promise.
- **Hebrews 9:15** — Christ is mediator of a new covenant through his death.
- **Hebrews 10:11–18** — Christ’s sacrifice secures the forgiveness promised in the new covenant.

## 8. Christ as covenant mediator and representative

Covenant theology centers on Christ as the mediator who fulfills covenant obligations and secures covenant blessings.

- **Isaiah 42:6** — The Servant is given “as a covenant for the people.”
- **Isaiah 49:8** — The Servant is appointed as a covenant to the people.
- **Matthew 26:28** — Jesus’ blood is “the blood of the covenant…for the forgiveness of sins.”
- **Romans 5:18–19** — Christ’s obedience makes many righteous.
- **1 Timothy 2:5** — Christ is the one mediator between God and man.
- **Hebrews 7:22** — Jesus is the guarantor of a better covenant.
- **Hebrews 12:24** — Jesus is the mediator of a new covenant.

## 9. One people of God in Christ

Covenant theology often argues that believing Jews and Gentiles are united into one covenant people.

- **John 10:16** — Jesus has other sheep who will become “one flock, one shepherd.”
- **Romans 11:17–24** — Gentiles are grafted into the olive tree of God’s covenant people.
- **Galatians 3:27–29** — In Christ, believers are Abraham’s offspring.
- **Ephesians 2:11–22** — Christ breaks down the dividing wall and creates one new man.
- **Ephesians 3:6** — Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise.
- **Philippians 3:3** — Believers in Christ are the true circumcision.
- **1 Peter 2:9–10** — New Covenant believers receive Old Testament covenant titles: chosen race, royal priesthood, holy nation.

## 10. Covenant signs and household principle

Reformed covenant theology also points to the inclusion of believers’ children in covenant administration.

- **Genesis 17:7–14** — The covenant sign is given to Abraham and his offspring.
- **Deuteronomy 29:10–13** — The covenant includes men, women, children, and sojourners.
