questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about the Lord's Supper?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Cor 11:23-26, Matt 26:26-28, Luke 22:19-20
questions.response:
The Bible teaches about the Lord’s Supper—also called Communion or the Eucharist—especially in these passages:

- **Matthew 26:26–29** — Jesus institutes the meal at the Last Supper: “This is my body… this is my blood of the covenant.”
- **Mark 14:22–25** — Mark’s account of the institution of the Lord’s Supper.
- **Luke 22:14–20** — Jesus says, “Do this in remembrance of me.”
- **1 Corinthians 10:16–17** — Paul teaches that the cup and bread are a “participation” or “communion” in the blood and body of Christ, and that believers are one body.
- **1 Corinthians 11:17–34** — The clearest extended teaching on the Lord’s Supper: its purpose, remembrance of Christ’s death, self-examination, and warnings against taking it wrongly.

Other related passages include:

- **Acts 2:42, 46** — The early church devoted itself to “the breaking of bread.”
- **Acts 20:7** — Christians gathered “to break bread” on the first day of the week.
- **John 6:35–58** — Jesus speaks of eating his flesh and drinking his blood; Christians differ on how directly this relates to the Lord’s Supper.

The central passage for doctrine and practice is **1 Corinthians 11:23–26**, where Paul writes:

> “For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you… ‘This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me’… ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood’… For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.”

questions.question: What passages address the doctrine of baptism?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 28:19, Acts 2:38-39, Rom 6:3-4, Col 2:11-12
questions.response:
Here are major Bible passages commonly used when studying the doctrine of baptism:

## Jesus’ Baptism and Teaching

- **Matthew 3:13–17** — Jesus is baptized by John; the Father speaks and the Spirit descends.
- **Mark 1:9–11** — Parallel account of Jesus’ baptism.
- **Luke 3:21–22** — Jesus’ baptism and the descent of the Spirit.
- **John 1:29–34** — John the Baptist testifies about Jesus and the Spirit descending on Him.
- **Matthew 28:18–20** — The Great Commission: disciples are to be baptized “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”
- **Mark 16:16** — “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved…”  
  *Note: this passage is textually debated in some manuscripts.*

## Baptism in Acts

- **Acts 2:38–41** — Peter calls people to repent and be baptized; about 3,000 are baptized.
- **Acts 8:12–13** — Samaritans believe and are baptized.
- **Acts 8:36–39** — The Ethiopian eunuch is baptized after confessing faith.
- **Acts 9:18** — Saul/Paul is baptized after his conversion.
- **Acts 10:44–48** — Cornelius and his household receive the Spirit and are baptized.
- **Acts 16:14–15** — Lydia and her household are baptized.
- **Acts 16:30–34** — The Philippian jailer and his household are baptized.
- **Acts 18:8** — Crispus and many Corinthians believe and are baptized.
- **Acts 19:1–7** — Disciples in Ephesus are baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus after knowing only John’s baptism.
- **Acts 22:16** — Ananias tells Paul, “Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name.”

## Baptism and Union with Christ

- **Romans 6:1–11** — Baptism signifies union with Christ in His death and resurrection.
- **Galatians 3:26–27** — “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.”
- **Colossians 2:11–12** — Baptism is connected with burial and resurrection with Christ through faith.
- **Ephesians 4:4–6** — “One Lord, one faith, one baptism.”

## Baptism, Cleansing, and Salvation Language

- **Titus 3:5** — “The washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit.”
- **Hebrews 10:22** — Hearts sprinkled clean and bodies washed with pure water.
- **1 Peter 3:18–22** — Baptism corresponds to Noah’s flood and is described as an appeal to God for a good conscience through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.

## John’s Baptism

- **Matthew 3:1–12** — John’s baptism of repentance.
- **Mark 1:4–8** — John baptizes for repentance and points to the One who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.
- **Luke 3:3–18** — John’s preaching and baptism.
- **John 3:22–30** — Jesus’ disciples baptize; John testifies that Christ must increase.
- **Acts 19:3–5** — John’s baptism distinguished from baptism in the name of Jesus.

## Baptism with the Holy Spirit

- **Matthew 3:11** — Jesus will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire.
- **Mark 1:8** — “He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.”
- **Luke 3:16** — John contrasts water baptism with the coming baptism of the Spirit.
- **John 1:33** — Jesus is identified as the One who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.
- **Acts 1:5** — Jesus promises the apostles will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.
- **Acts 11:15–16** — Peter connects Cornelius’s experience with Jesus’ promise of Spirit baptism.
- **1 Corinthians 12:13** — “In one Spirit we were all baptized into one body.”

## Possible Old Testament Foreshadowing / Typology

- **Genesis 6–9** — Noah and the flood, later connected to baptism in **1 Peter 3:20–21**.
- **Exodus 14** — Israel passes through the Red Sea.
- **1 Corinthians 10:1–2** — Paul says Israel was “baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.”
- **Ezekiel 36:25–27** — God promises cleansing with water and the gift of the Spirit.

These passages are central to discussions about baptism’s meaning, subjects, mode, relation to faith and repentance, connection with the Holy Spirit, and its place in the church’s mission.

questions.question: Where does Scripture teach about church government and eldership?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Tim 3:1-7, Titus 1:5-9, Acts 14:23, 1 Pet 5:1-4
questions.response:
Scripture teaches about church government and eldership especially in the New Testament. The main passages are these:

## 1. Christ is the Head of the Church

All church authority is under Christ.

- **Ephesians 1:22–23** — God “put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church.”
- **Colossians 1:18** — Christ “is the head of the body, the church.”
- **Matthew 28:18–20** — Christ has all authority and commissions the church to make disciples.

## 2. Elders Appointed in Local Churches

The apostles appointed elders to lead local congregations.

- **Acts 14:23** — Paul and Barnabas “appointed elders for them in every church.”
- **Titus 1:5** — Titus was told to “appoint elders in every town.”
- **Acts 20:17** — Paul called the “elders of the church” in Ephesus.

These texts show that local churches were ordinarily led by elders, often in plurality.

## 3. Elders Are Also Called Overseers and Shepherds/Pastors

The New Testament uses several terms for the same office or closely related functions:

- **Elder** emphasizes maturity and dignity.
- **Overseer/Bishop** emphasizes oversight and governance.
- **Pastor/Shepherd** emphasizes care and feeding of the flock.

Key texts:

- **Acts 20:17, 28** — Paul calls the Ephesian “elders” and tells them the Holy Spirit made them “overseers” to “care for” or shepherd the church.
- **Titus 1:5–7** — Paul speaks of appointing “elders,” then immediately calls such a man an “overseer.”
- **1 Peter 5:1–4** — Peter exhorts the “elders” to “shepherd the flock of God” and exercise oversight.

## 4. Qualifications for Elders

The clearest qualifications are given in:

- **1 Timothy 3:1–7** — qualifications for an overseer.
- **Titus 1:5–9** — qualifications for elders/overseers.

These include being above reproach, faithful in marriage, sober-minded, self-controlled, hospitable, able to teach, not violent, not greedy, managing one’s household well, and holding firmly to sound doctrine.

## 5. Duties of Elders

Elders are called to lead, teach, shepherd, protect, and care for the church.

- **Acts 20:28–31** — elders must shepherd the church and guard it from false teachers.
- **1 Peter 5:1–4** — elders shepherd willingly, eagerly, and as examples, not domineering.
- **1 Timothy 5:17** — elders “rule well,” especially those who labor in preaching and teaching.
- **Titus 1:9** — elders must teach sound doctrine and rebuke those who contradict it.
- **James 5:14** — the sick are to call for the elders of the church to pray over them.

## 6. The Church’s Response to Leaders

Members are called to respect, follow, and submit to faithful church leaders.

- **Hebrews 13:7** — “Remember your leaders, those who spoke to you the word of God.”
- **Hebrews 13:17** — “Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are keeping watch over your souls.”
- **1 Thessalonians 5:12–13** — respect those who labor among you and are over you in the Lord.

## 7. Accountability and Discipline of Elders

Elders have authority, but they are also accountable.

- **1 Timothy 5:19–22** — accusations against elders require witnesses; sinning elders are to be rebuked publicly.
- **1 Peter 5:3** — elders must not be domineering over those in their charge.
- **Acts 20:28** — elders must first “pay careful attention” to themselves.

## 8. Deacons as Another Recognized Office

Alongside elders/overseers, Scripture also teaches about deacons.

- **Philippians 1:1** — Paul addresses “overseers and deacons.”
- **1 Timothy 3:8–13** — qualifications for deacons.
- **Acts 6:1–6** — often seen as a prototype for diaconal service, though the term “deacon” is not used there.

## 9. Congregational Involvement and Church Discipline

Scripture also shows the congregation involved in important matters.

- **Matthew 18:15–20** — unresolved sin is to be brought before “the church.”
- **1 Corinthians 5:1–13** — the church acts in discipline against open, unrepentant sin.
- **Acts 6:1–6** — the congregation selects qualified men, whom the apostles appoint.
- **Acts 15** — apostles and elders deliberate over doctrinal controversy, with the church involved.

## Summary

The main biblical passages on church government and eldership are:

- **Acts 14:23**
- **Acts 20:17–31**
- **Philippians 1:1**
- **1 Timothy 3:1–13**
- **1 Timothy 5:17–22**
- **Titus 1:5–9**
- **1 Peter 5:1–4**
- **Hebrews 13:7, 17**
- **James 5:14**

In short, Scripture teaches that Christ is the Head of the church, local churches are to be led by qualified elders/overseers who shepherd and teach, deacons serve the church, leaders are accountable, and the congregation also has responsibilities in the life and discipline of the church.

questions.question: What Bible passages teach about the second coming of Christ?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Acts 1:11, 1 Thess 4:16-17, Matt 24:30, Rev 1:7
questions.response:
Here are major Bible passages that teach about the **second coming of Christ**—His future return in glory to judge, reign, and complete salvation for His people.

## Key passages in the Gospels

- **Matthew 24:27–31** — Jesus says His coming will be visible and glorious, like lightning, and that He will gather His elect.
- **Matthew 24:36–44** — No one knows the day or hour; believers must be watchful and ready.
- **Matthew 25:31–46** — The Son of Man comes in glory, sits on His throne, and judges the nations.
- **Mark 13:24–27, 32–37** — Christ returns after tribulation with power and glory; His followers must stay awake.
- **Luke 12:35–40** — Jesus compares His return to a master coming home unexpectedly.
- **Luke 21:25–28** — Signs in heaven and earth precede the coming of the Son of Man; believers should lift up their heads because redemption is near.
- **John 14:1–3** — Jesus promises to come again and take His disciples to Himself.

## In Acts

- **Acts 1:9–11** — Angels tell the disciples that Jesus will return in the same way He ascended into heaven.
- **Acts 3:19–21** — Peter speaks of the time when God will send Christ and restore all things.

## In Paul’s letters

- **1 Thessalonians 4:13–18** — The Lord descends from heaven; the dead in Christ rise first; believers are caught up to meet the Lord.
- **1 Thessalonians 5:1–11** — The day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night; believers should be sober and prepared.
- **2 Thessalonians 1:7–10** — Jesus is revealed from heaven with mighty angels, bringing judgment and glory.
- **2 Thessalonians 2:1–12** — Paul discusses events connected with Christ’s coming and the “man of lawlessness.”
- **1 Corinthians 1:7–8** — Believers wait for the revealing of Jesus Christ.
- **1 Corinthians 15:22–28, 50–58** — At Christ’s coming, the dead are raised and death is defeated.
- **Philippians 3:20–21** — Christ will return from heaven and transform believers’ bodies.
- **Colossians 3:4** — When Christ appears, believers will appear with Him in glory.
- **Titus 2:11–14** — Christians wait for the “blessed hope,” the appearing of the glory of Christ.

## In the General Epistles

- **Hebrews 9:27–28** — Christ will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save those eagerly waiting for Him.
- **James 5:7–9** — Believers are called to be patient because the coming of the Lord is near.
- **1 Peter 1:7, 13** — Hope is fixed on the revelation of Jesus Christ.
- **1 Peter 4:7** — “The end of all things is at hand”; believers should be self-controlled and prayerful.
- **2 Peter 3:3–13** — Scoffers will deny His coming, but the day of the Lord will come; believers await new heavens and a new earth.
- **1 John 2:28** — Believers should abide in Christ so they may have confidence when He appears.
- **1 John 3:2–3** — When Christ appears, believers will be like Him.
- **Jude 14–15** — The Lord comes with His holy ones to execute judgment.

## In Revelation

- **Revelation 1:7** — “Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him.”
- **Revelation 3:11** — “I am coming soon.”
- **Revelation 19:11–21** — Christ appears as the victorious King and Judge.
- **Revelation 20:11–15** — Final judgment before the great white throne.
- **Revelation 21:1–5** — New heaven and new earth; God dwells with His people.
- **Revelation 22:7, 12, 20** — Jesus repeatedly says, “I am coming soon.”

## Old Testament background passages often connected to His coming

- **Daniel 7:13–14** — The “Son of Man” comes with the clouds and receives everlasting dominion.
- **Zechariah 12:10** — They look on the one they have pierced and mourn.
- **Zechariah 14:1–9** — The Lord comes in victory and reigns as King over all the earth.
- **Malachi 3:1–5** — The Lord comes to His temple and purifies/judges.
- **Malachi 4:1–6** — The day of the Lord brings judgment and healing.

A concise summary would be: **Christ will return personally, visibly, gloriously, unexpectedly, and victoriously; He will raise the dead, judge the world, save His people, defeat evil, and bring God’s kingdom to its fullness.**

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about the final judgment?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 25:31-46, Rev 20:11-15, 2 Cor 5:10, Acts 17:31
questions.response:
The Bible teaches about the final judgment in many places. Key passages include:

### Old Testament

- **Ecclesiastes 12:14** — “God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil.”
- **Daniel 7:9–14** — A heavenly court is pictured, with books opened and the “Son of Man” receiving an everlasting kingdom.
- **Daniel 12:2** — Speaks of resurrection: some to everlasting life, others to shame and everlasting contempt.

### Teachings of Jesus

- **Matthew 25:31–46** — The judgment of the nations, often called the “sheep and goats” judgment. The Son of Man separates the righteous from the wicked.
- **Matthew 12:36–37** — People will give account for every careless word.
- **John 5:28–29** — Jesus says all who are in the tombs will rise, some to the resurrection of life and others to judgment.
- **John 12:48** — Jesus’ words will judge people on the last day.

### Apostolic Teaching

- **Acts 17:30–31** — God has fixed a day to judge the world in righteousness through the man He has appointed, Jesus Christ.
- **Romans 2:5–16** — Paul teaches that God will judge people according to their deeds and secrets through Christ.
- **Romans 14:10–12** — “We will all stand before the judgment seat of God.”
- **2 Corinthians 5:10** — “We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ.”
- **Hebrews 9:27** — “It is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment.”
- **2 Peter 3:7–13** — Speaks of the day of judgment and the renewal of heaven and earth.
- **Jude 14–15** — The Lord comes to execute judgment on all.

### Revelation

- **Revelation 20:11–15** — The “great white throne” judgment. The dead are judged according to what is written in the books, and anyone not found in the book of life is cast into the lake of fire.
- **Revelation 22:12** — Jesus says, “I am coming soon, bringing my recompense with me, to repay each one for what he has done.”

In summary, the Bible teaches that there will be a final judgment in which God, through Jesus Christ, will judge all people, reveal what is hidden, vindicate the righteous, condemn evil, and bring in the fullness of His kingdom.

questions.question: What Scripture passages teach about heaven and hell?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rev 21:1-4, Matt 25:46, 2 Thess 1:9, John 14:2-3
questions.response:
Here are major Scripture passages commonly cited about **heaven** and **hell**, with brief notes on what they teach.

## Passages about Heaven / Eternal Life

- **John 14:1–3** — Jesus says He is preparing a place for His people in His Father’s house.
- **Revelation 21:1–4** — The new heaven and new earth; God dwells with His people; no more death, mourning, crying, or pain.
- **Revelation 22:1–5** — The restored creation, the river of life, the tree of life, and God’s servants reigning with Him.
- **1 Corinthians 2:9** — God has prepared things beyond human imagination for those who love Him.
- **Philippians 3:20–21** — Believers’ citizenship is in heaven, and Christ will transform their bodies.
- **2 Corinthians 5:1–8** — Being “at home with the Lord” after death.
- **1 Thessalonians 4:13–18** — The resurrection of believers and being with the Lord forever.
- **Matthew 6:19–21** — Storing up treasures in heaven.
- **Matthew 25:34** — The righteous inherit the kingdom prepared for them.
- **Luke 23:42–43** — Jesus tells the repentant thief, “Today you will be with me in paradise.”
- **Hebrews 11:13–16** — God’s people seek a “better country,” a heavenly one.
- **1 Peter 1:3–5** — An imperishable inheritance kept in heaven.

## Passages about Hell / Judgment

- **Matthew 25:41, 46** — Jesus speaks of eternal punishment and eternal life.
- **Mark 9:43–48** — Jesus warns about Gehenna, where “the fire is not quenched.”
- **Matthew 10:28** — God can destroy both soul and body in hell.
- **Luke 16:19–31** — The rich man and Lazarus; a picture of torment after death.
- **Revelation 20:11–15** — The final judgment and the lake of fire.
- **Revelation 21:8** — The second death described as the lake of fire.
- **2 Thessalonians 1:7–10** — Those who reject God face judgment and exclusion from the presence of the Lord.
- **Daniel 12:2** — Resurrection to everlasting life or to shame and everlasting contempt.
- **John 5:28–29** — Resurrection of life and resurrection of judgment.
- **Matthew 13:40–42, 49–50** — Jesus’ parables describe final separation and judgment.
- **Jude 6–7** — Judgment described with eternal fire imagery.
- **2 Peter 2:4–9** — God’s judgment on the wicked and rescue of the righteous.

## Passages Showing the Choice Between Life and Judgment

- **John 3:16–18** — Whoever believes in Christ has eternal life; whoever does not believe is condemned already.
- **Romans 6:23** — “The wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
- **Matthew 7:13–14** — The narrow way leads to life; the broad way leads to destruction.
- **Galatians 6:7–8** — Sowing to the flesh leads to corruption; sowing to the Spirit leads to eternal life.

Different Christian traditions interpret some details differently, especially the nature of hell, but these are among the central biblical passages used in discussions of heaven, hell, eternal life, and final judgment.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach the doctrine of creation?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gen 1:1, John 1:3, Col 1:16, Heb 11:3
questions.response:
The Bible teaches the doctrine of creation throughout Scripture, not only in Genesis. Key passages include:

### 1. Genesis: the foundational creation account
- **Genesis 1:1** — “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.”
- **Genesis 1–2** — God creates all things by his word, orders creation, makes it good, and creates humanity in his image.
- **Genesis 2:7** — God forms man from the dust and gives him life.

### 2. The Psalms: creation by God’s word and power
- **Psalm 33:6, 9** — “By the word of the LORD the heavens were made… For he spoke, and it came to be.”
- **Psalm 90:2** — God exists before creation: “Before the mountains were brought forth… from everlasting to everlasting you are God.”
- **Psalm 104** — A hymn celebrating God as Creator and sustainer of the world.

### 3. The Prophets: God alone is Creator
- **Isaiah 40:26, 28** — God created the stars and is “the Creator of the ends of the earth.”
- **Isaiah 42:5** — God “created the heavens… spread out the earth.”
- **Isaiah 45:12, 18** — God made the earth and formed it to be inhabited.
- **Jeremiah 10:12** — God made the earth by his power and wisdom.

### 4. The Gospels and New Testament: creation through Christ
- **John 1:1–3** — “All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made.”
- **Colossians 1:16–17** — All things were created through Christ and for Christ, and in him all things hold together.
- **Hebrews 1:2–3** — God made the world through the Son, who upholds all things.
- **1 Corinthians 8:6** — “One God, the Father, from whom are all things… and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.”

### 5. Creation out of nothing
- **Hebrews 11:3** — “The universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible.”
- **Romans 4:17** — God “calls into existence the things that do not exist.”

### 6. Revelation: creation for God’s glory
- **Revelation 4:11** — “You created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.”

In summary, the doctrine of creation is taught especially in **Genesis 1–2**, but it is reaffirmed across the whole Bible: God created all things, by his word, through the Son, by his will, out of nothing, and for his glory.

questions.question: What passages teach about God's providence?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 10:29-31, Rom 8:28, Eph 1:11, Dan 4:35
questions.response:
Here are key Bible passages that teach about **God’s providence**—his sovereign, wise, and purposeful governing of creation and human history.

## God rules over all things

- **Psalm 103:19** — “The LORD has established his throne in the heavens, and his kingdom rules over all.”
- **Psalm 115:3** — God does whatever he pleases.
- **Daniel 4:34–35** — God rules over the kingdoms of men; none can stop his hand.
- **Ephesians 1:11** — God “works all things according to the counsel of his will.”
- **Colossians 1:16–17** — All things were created through Christ and for him, and “in him all things hold together.”
- **Hebrews 1:3** — Christ “upholds the universe by the word of his power.”

## God cares for creation

- **Psalm 104** — A poetic description of God sustaining animals, waters, seasons, and the earth.
- **Psalm 145:15–16** — God opens his hand and satisfies the desire of every living thing.
- **Matthew 6:25–34** — Jesus teaches that the Father feeds the birds and clothes the lilies; therefore believers should trust him.
- **Matthew 10:29–31** — Not even a sparrow falls apart from the Father’s will; believers are of great value to him.
- **Acts 17:24–28** — God gives life and breath to all and determines times and places.

## God governs human plans and actions

- **Proverbs 16:9** — “The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps.”
- **Proverbs 19:21** — Many are the plans in a person’s heart, but the Lord’s purpose stands.
- **Proverbs 21:1** — The king’s heart is in the hand of the Lord.
- **James 4:13–15** — Human plans should be made humbly: “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.”

## God uses evil and suffering for his purposes

- **Genesis 50:20** — Joseph tells his brothers: “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.”
- **Job 1–2; 38–42** — Job’s suffering occurs within God’s sovereign permission, though Job does not fully understand it.
- **Isaiah 45:5–7** — God declares his sovereign rule over light and darkness, well-being and calamity.
- **Acts 2:23** — Jesus was crucified according to God’s definite plan and foreknowledge, though human beings were responsible.
- **Acts 4:27–28** — Herod, Pilate, Gentiles, and Israel did what God’s hand and plan had predestined.
- **Romans 8:28** — God works all things together for good for those who love him.

## God provides for his people

- **Genesis 22:14** — “The LORD will provide.”
- **Exodus 16** — God provides manna in the wilderness.
- **Deuteronomy 8:2–4** — God sustained Israel in the wilderness to teach dependence on him.
- **1 Kings 17:8–16** — God provides for Elijah through the widow of Zarephath.
- **Philippians 4:19** — “My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.”

## God directs history toward his saving purpose

- **Isaiah 46:9–10** — God declares the end from the beginning, saying, “My counsel shall stand.”
- **Romans 11:33–36** — God’s wisdom and ways are unsearchable; all things are from him, through him, and to him.
- **Galatians 4:4–5** — “When the fullness of time had come,” God sent his Son.
- **Revelation 21–22** — History ends with God’s promised new creation.

## A concise summary passage

**Romans 8:28–39** is one of the clearest passages on providence: God works all things for the good of his people, conforms them to Christ, and nothing can separate them from his love.

questions.question: Where does Scripture teach about the nature and practice of prayer?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 6:9-13, Phil 4:6, 1 Thess 5:17, John 14:13-14
questions.response:
Scripture teaches about the nature and practice of prayer throughout both Testaments. Key passages include:

### 1. Prayer as calling on God in faith
- **Genesis 4:26** — people “began to call upon the name of the LORD.”
- **Psalm 50:15** — “Call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you.”
- **Jeremiah 33:3** — “Call to me and I will answer you.”
- **Hebrews 11:6** — prayer requires faith that God exists and rewards those who seek him.

### 2. The Psalms as a school of prayer
- **Psalm 5:1–3** — morning prayer and watchful waiting.
- **Psalm 23** — trust in the Lord’s care.
- **Psalm 51** — confession and repentance.
- **Psalm 63** — longing for God.
- **Psalm 86** — petition, praise, and dependence.
- **Psalm 145** — adoration and thanksgiving.

### 3. Jesus’ teaching on prayer
- **Matthew 6:5–13** — pray sincerely, not for show; includes the Lord’s Prayer.
- **Luke 11:1–13** — Jesus teaches the Lord’s Prayer and encourages persistence.
- **Matthew 7:7–11** — “Ask, and it will be given to you.”
- **Matthew 26:36–46** — Jesus prays in Gethsemane, submitting to the Father’s will.
- **John 14:13–14; 15:7; 16:23–24** — prayer in Jesus’ name.
- **John 17** — Jesus’ high-priestly prayer.

### 4. Prayer as continual dependence on God
- **1 Thessalonians 5:16–18** — “Pray without ceasing.”
- **Ephesians 6:18** — pray “at all times in the Spirit.”
- **Colossians 4:2** — “Continue steadfastly in prayer.”
- **Romans 12:12** — be “constant in prayer.”

### 5. Prayer with thanksgiving
- **Philippians 4:6–7** — present requests to God “with thanksgiving,” receiving his peace.
- **Colossians 3:17** — do everything with thanksgiving to God.
- **1 Timothy 2:1** — prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings for all people.

### 6. Prayer of confession and repentance
- **Psalm 32:5** — confessing sin to the Lord.
- **Proverbs 28:13** — confession and forsaking sin bring mercy.
- **Daniel 9:3–19** — Daniel’s prayer of confession.
- **1 John 1:9** — God forgives and cleanses those who confess their sins.

### 7. Prayer according to God’s will
- **Matthew 6:10** — “Your will be done.”
- **1 John 5:14–15** — confidence when we ask according to God’s will.
- **James 4:3** — warning against selfish motives in prayer.
- **Matthew 26:39** — “Not as I will, but as you will.”

### 8. Prayer through Christ and by the Spirit
- **John 14:6** — access to the Father is through Christ.
- **Ephesians 2:18** — through Christ we have access to the Father by the Spirit.
- **Romans 8:26–27** — the Spirit helps us in our weakness and intercedes for us.
- **Hebrews 4:14–16** — we approach God’s throne of grace through our great High Priest.

### 9. Prayer for others
- **1 Timothy 2:1–4** — pray for all people and those in authority.
- **Ephesians 1:15–23; 3:14–21** — Paul’s prayers for the church.
- **Colossians 1:9–14** — prayer for spiritual growth.
- **James 5:14–18** — prayer for the sick and the power of righteous prayer.

### 10. Examples of prayer in Scripture
- **Hannah** — prayer of distress and dedication: **1 Samuel 1–2**
- **Solomon** — prayer for wisdom: **1 Kings 3:5–14**
- **Elijah** — prayer and God’s power: **1 Kings 18:36–39; James 5:17–18**
- **Nehemiah** — brief, practical prayer: **Nehemiah 1:4–11; 2:4**
- **Daniel** — regular prayer: **Daniel 6:10**
- **The early church** — gathered prayer: **Acts 1:14; 2:42; 4:23–31; 12:5**

In summary, Scripture teaches that prayer is humble, faithful communion with God—adoring him, confessing sin, giving thanks, asking for help, interceding for others, and submitting to his will through Christ and by the Holy Spirit.

questions.question: What Bible passages relate to Sabbath observance?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Exod 20:8-11, Isa 58:13-14, Mark 2:27-28, Heb 4:9-10
questions.response:
Here are major Bible passages related to Sabbath observance, grouped by theme.

## 1. Creation and the Sabbath Pattern

- **Genesis 2:1–3** — God rests on the seventh day and blesses/sanctifies it.
- **Exodus 20:8–11** — The Sabbath command is grounded in God’s creation rest.

## 2. The Ten Commandments

- **Exodus 20:8–11** — “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.”
- **Deuteronomy 5:12–15** — “Observe the Sabbath day”; connected with Israel’s deliverance from Egypt.

## 3. Sabbath Before Sinai

- **Exodus 16:22–30** — Manna is not gathered on the seventh day; the Sabbath is observed before the giving of the Ten Commandments.

## 4. Sabbath as a Sign of the Covenant

- **Exodus 31:12–17** — Sabbath is a sign between God and Israel.
- **Ezekiel 20:12, 20** — Sabbaths are given as a sign to know the Lord sanctifies His people.

## 5. Sabbath Laws and Instructions

- **Exodus 23:10–12** — Rest for people, servants, animals; linked with the sabbatical year.
- **Exodus 34:21** — Rest even during plowing and harvest.
- **Leviticus 23:1–3** — Sabbath listed among the appointed times of the Lord.
- **Numbers 15:32–36** — Case of a man gathering sticks on the Sabbath.
- **Numbers 28:9–10** — Special Sabbath offerings.
- **Deuteronomy 5:14** — Sabbath rest includes servants, foreigners, and animals.

## 6. Sabbath and Justice/Mercy

- **Isaiah 56:1–8** — Blessing for those who keep the Sabbath, including foreigners.
- **Isaiah 58:13–14** — Calling the Sabbath a delight and honoring it.
- **Jeremiah 17:19–27** — Warning against carrying burdens on the Sabbath.
- **Nehemiah 13:15–22** — Nehemiah reforms Sabbath-breaking commerce.

## 7. Sabbath in the Prophets

- **Ezekiel 22:26** — Priests accused of profaning the Sabbaths.
- **Ezekiel 23:38** — Profaning the sanctuary and Sabbaths.
- **Amos 8:4–6** — Critique of merchants eager for the Sabbath to end.
- **Hosea 2:11** — Sabbaths mentioned among Israel’s festivals and appointed times.

## 8. Sabbath in the Gospels: Jesus and the Sabbath

- **Matthew 12:1–14** — Jesus’ disciples pluck grain; Jesus heals on the Sabbath.
- **Mark 2:23–28** — “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.”
- **Mark 3:1–6** — Jesus heals a man with a withered hand on the Sabbath.
- **Luke 4:16** — Jesus attends synagogue on the Sabbath.
- **Luke 6:1–11** — Grain-plucking and healing on the Sabbath.
- **Luke 13:10–17** — Jesus heals a crippled woman on the Sabbath.
- **Luke 14:1–6** — Jesus heals a man with dropsy on the Sabbath.
- **John 5:1–18** — Healing at Bethesda on the Sabbath.
- **John 7:22–24** — Circumcision and Sabbath reasoning.
- **John 9:1–16** — Healing the man born blind on the Sabbath.

## 9. Sabbath in Acts

- **Acts 13:14, 42–44** — Paul speaks in the synagogue on the Sabbath.
- **Acts 16:13** — Prayer gathering on the Sabbath.
- **Acts 17:2** — Paul reasons in the synagogue on three Sabbaths.
- **Acts 18:4** — Paul reasons in the synagogue every Sabbath.

## 10. Sabbath and Christian Interpretation

- **Romans 14:5–6** — Some regard one day above another; others regard all days alike.
- **Colossians 2:16–17** — Let no one judge you regarding Sabbath days; they are a shadow pointing to Christ.
- **Galatians 4:9–11** — Paul warns about bondage to observing days, months, seasons, and years.
- **Hebrews 4:1–11** — Speaks of a “Sabbath rest” for the people of God.
- **Revelation 1:10** — “The Lord’s Day” mentioned, often discussed in relation to Christian worship.

## Related Themes

- **Sabbatical year:** Exodus 23:10–11; Leviticus 25:1–7; Deuteronomy 15:1–11  
- **Year of Jubilee:** Leviticus 25:8–17  
- **Festival “sabbaths” or days of rest:** Leviticus 23:7–8, 24, 27–32, 39  

These passages cover the Sabbath as creation pattern, commandment, covenant sign, social rest, prophetic concern, Jesus’ teaching and practice, and later Christian reflection.

questions.question: Where are the Ten Commandments given in Scripture?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Exod 20:1-17, Deut 5:6-21
questions.response:
The Ten Commandments are given in two main places in Scripture:

1. **Exodus 20:1–17** — God gives them to Israel at Mount Sinai.  
2. **Deuteronomy 5:6–21** — Moses repeats them to the next generation before entering the Promised Land.

They are also referred to as the “Ten Commandments” or “ten words” in passages such as:

- **Exodus 34:28**
- **Deuteronomy 4:13**
- **Deuteronomy 10:4**

Related passages about the tablets include **Exodus 31:18**, **Exodus 32**, and **Exodus 34**.

questions.question: Where does Jesus teach the Lord's Prayer?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 6:9-13, Luke 11:2-4
questions.response:
Jesus teaches the Lord’s Prayer in two Gospel passages:

- **Matthew 6:9–13** — during the **Sermon on the Mount**, as part of his teaching on prayer.  
- **Luke 11:1–4** — after one of his disciples asks, “Lord, teach us to pray.”

In Matthew it begins, **“Our Father in heaven…”**; in Luke it is a shorter version beginning, **“Father…”**

questions.question: What passages address the sacraments in Reformed theology?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 28:19, 1 Cor 11:23-26, Acts 2:38-39, Rom 6:3-4
questions.response:
In Reformed theology, the sacraments are usually understood as **holy signs and seals of the covenant of grace**, instituted by Christ, to represent Christ and his benefits and to strengthen faith. Reformed churches recognize **two sacraments: Baptism and the Lord’s Supper**.

## Key biblical passages

### 1. General sacramental themes: signs, seals, covenant

- **Genesis 17:7–14** — Circumcision as the covenant sign under Abraham.  
- **Romans 4:11** — Circumcision called a “sign” and “seal” of righteousness by faith.  
- **Exodus 12** — The Passover as a covenant meal pointing forward to redemption.  
- **1 Corinthians 10:1–4** — Israel’s “baptism” in the sea and spiritual food/drink, often used in Reformed sacramental theology.  
- **Colossians 2:11–12** — Circumcision and baptism connected covenantally.  
- **Hebrews 9–10** — Old covenant rites fulfilled in Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice.

## Baptism

- **Matthew 28:18–20** — Christ commands baptism in the triune name.  
- **Acts 2:38–39** — Baptism, forgiveness, the Spirit, and the promise “for you and for your children.”  
- **Acts 8:12–13, 36–38** — Baptism of professing believers.  
- **Acts 10:44–48** — Gentiles baptized after receiving the Spirit.  
- **Acts 16:14–15, 31–34** — Household baptisms: Lydia and the Philippian jailer.  
- **Romans 6:3–4** — Baptism signifies union with Christ in his death and resurrection.  
- **Galatians 3:26–29** — Baptism and being clothed with Christ.  
- **Ephesians 4:4–6** — “One Lord, one faith, one baptism.”  
- **Titus 3:5** — Washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit.  
- **1 Peter 3:20–21** — Baptism as an appeal to God through Christ’s resurrection.

## The Lord’s Supper

- **Matthew 26:26–29** — Institution of the Supper.  
- **Mark 14:22–25** — Institution of the Supper.  
- **Luke 22:14–20** — “This is my body… this cup… the new covenant in my blood.”  
- **John 6:35–58** — Eating Christ’s flesh and drinking his blood; important in discussions of spiritual feeding, though not an institution narrative.  
- **Acts 2:42** — The early church devoted itself to “the breaking of bread.”  
- **Acts 20:7** — The church gathered to break bread on the first day of the week.  
- **1 Corinthians 10:16–17** — The cup and bread as participation, or communion, in Christ’s blood and body.  
- **1 Corinthians 11:17–34** — Paul’s major teaching on the Lord’s Supper, including self-examination and warning against unworthy participation.

## Major Reformed confessional passages

If you mean **Reformed confessional documents**, the main sections are:

- **Westminster Confession of Faith**
  - Chapter 27: “Of the Sacraments”
  - Chapter 28: “Of Baptism”
  - Chapter 29: “Of the Lord’s Supper”

- **Westminster Larger Catechism**
  - Q. 161–177, on sacraments, baptism, and the Lord’s Supper

- **Westminster Shorter Catechism**
  - Q. 91–97

- **Heidelberg Catechism**
  - Q. 65–68, on the sacraments generally
  - Q. 69–74, on baptism
  - Q. 75–82, on the Lord’s Supper

- **Belgic Confession**
  - Article 33: The Sacraments
  - Article 34: Baptism
  - Article 35: The Lord’s Supper

- **Second Helvetic Confession**
  - Chapter 19: The Sacraments
  - Chapter 20: Baptism
  - Chapter 21: The Lord’s Supper

In summary, the central biblical passages are **Matthew 28:18–20** for baptism, **Matthew 26/Luke 22/1 Corinthians 11** for the Lord’s Supper, and **Romans 4:11, Colossians 2:11–12, and 1 Corinthians 10:16–17** for broader Reformed sacramental theology.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about church discipline?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 18:15-17, 1 Cor 5:1-13, Titus 3:10, 2 Thess 3:14-15
questions.response:
The Bible teaches about church discipline in several key places. The clearest and most central passages are:

## 1. Matthew 18:15–20 — The basic process
Jesus gives a step-by-step pattern for dealing with a sinning brother or sister:

1. Go privately and show them their fault.
2. If they will not listen, take one or two others.
3. If they still refuse, tell it to the church.
4. If they refuse even the church, treat them “as a Gentile and a tax collector.”

This passage shows that discipline should begin privately and aim at repentance and restoration.

## 2. 1 Corinthians 5 — Serious public sin
Paul rebukes the Corinthian church for tolerating open sexual immorality. He tells them to remove the unrepentant person from fellowship:

> “Purge the evil person from among you.”  
> — 1 Corinthians 5:13

This passage shows that church discipline protects the holiness of the church and can involve exclusion from fellowship when sin is serious and unrepented of.

## 3. 2 Corinthians 2:5–11 — Restoration after repentance
Paul later urges the church to forgive and comfort a disciplined person who appears to have repented:

> “You should rather turn to forgive and comfort him.”  
> — 2 Corinthians 2:7

This shows that the goal of discipline is not punishment for its own sake, but restoration.

## 4. Galatians 6:1 — Restore gently
Paul says:

> “If anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness.”

This emphasizes humility, gentleness, and self-watchfulness in correcting others.

## 5. 2 Thessalonians 3:6, 14–15 — Warning and limited association
Paul instructs believers to keep away from someone walking in disobedience, but adds:

> “Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother.”  
> — 2 Thessalonians 3:15

This shows that discipline should be firm but loving.

## 6. Titus 3:10–11 — Divisive people
Paul tells Titus:

> “As for a person who stirs up division, after warning him once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him.”

This applies especially to divisive behavior in the church.

## 7. 1 Timothy 5:19–20 — Discipline of elders
Paul gives instructions about accusations against elders and says persistent sin may require public rebuke:

> “As for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all.”

This shows that church leaders are also accountable.

## Summary

The Bible teaches that church discipline should be:

- **Biblical** — based on God’s Word, not personal preference.
- **Loving** — seeking the sinner’s repentance and restoration.
- **Patient and careful** — beginning privately when possible.
- **Protective** — guarding the church from serious, unrepentant sin.
- **Restorative** — ready to forgive when repentance occurs.

The main passages are **Matthew 18:15–20**, **1 Corinthians 5**, **2 Corinthians 2:5–11**, **Galatians 6:1**, **2 Thessalonians 3:6–15**, **Titus 3:10–11**, and **1 Timothy 5:19–20**.

questions.question: What Scripture passages teach about Christian liberty?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gal 5:1, 1 Cor 8:9, Rom 14:1-23, 1 Pet 2:16
questions.response:
Here are key Scripture passages that teach about **Christian liberty**—freedom in Christ from sin’s dominion, from condemnation, from man-made religious bondage, and freedom to serve God in love.

## Core Passages on Christian Liberty

### **John 8:31–36**
Jesus teaches that true freedom comes through Him:  
> “If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.”  
This is freedom from slavery to sin.

### **Galatians 5:1**
> “For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.”  
Paul warns believers not to return to bondage under the law as a means of justification.

### **Galatians 5:13**
> “You were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another.”  
Christian liberty is not license to sin; it is freedom to love and serve.

### **Romans 6:14–22**
> “Sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.”  
Believers are freed from sin’s mastery and become servants of righteousness.

### **Romans 8:1–4**
> “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”  
Christ frees believers from condemnation and the inability of the law to justify.

### **2 Corinthians 3:17**
> “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.”  
The Spirit brings freedom from spiritual blindness and bondage.

## Liberty and the Conscience

### **Romans 14:1–23**
Paul teaches that Christians may differ on disputable matters such as food and days. Believers should not despise or judge one another over matters of conscience.

Key verse:  
> “Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind.” — Romans 14:5

### **1 Corinthians 8:1–13**
Paul discusses food offered to idols and teaches that knowledge of liberty must be governed by love for weaker brothers.

Key verse:  
> “Take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak.” — 1 Corinthians 8:9

### **1 Corinthians 10:23–33**
> “All things are lawful,” but not all things are helpful.  
Christian liberty must seek God’s glory and the good of others.

### **Colossians 2:16–23**
> “Let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath.”  
Paul warns against human regulations and ascetic rules that appear spiritual but cannot transform the heart.

## Freedom from Legalism

### **Acts 15:1–29**
The Jerusalem Council addresses whether Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. The apostles reject placing that burden on them.

Key verse:  
> “Why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples…?” — Acts 15:10

### **Galatians 2:4–5**
Paul resists false brothers who tried to “spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus” and bring believers into slavery.

### **Galatians 3:23–26**
The law served as a guardian until Christ, but believers are now justified by faith and are sons of God through faith in Christ.

### **Galatians 4:8–11**
Paul warns against returning to “weak and worthless elementary principles” through religious observances treated as necessary for acceptance with God.

## Liberty Used Righteously

### **1 Peter 2:16**
> “Live as people who are free, not using your freedom as a cover-up for evil, but living as servants of God.”  
Freedom in Christ is not independence from God but joyful service to Him.

### **James 1:25**
> “The perfect law, the law of liberty…”  
God’s Word is called the law of liberty because obedience to God is true freedom.

### **James 2:12**
> “So speak and so act as those who are to be judged under the law of liberty.”  
Christian liberty is accountable to God’s moral will.

### **1 Timothy 4:1–5**
Paul warns against false teaching that forbids marriage or requires abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving.

## Summary

Christian liberty includes freedom:

- **From sin’s dominion** — Romans 6:14; John 8:36  
- **From condemnation** — Romans 8:1  
- **From justification by law-keeping** — Galatians 5:1  
- **From man-made religious rules** — Colossians 2:16–23  
- **To serve God and others in love** — Galatians 5:13; 1 Peter 2:16  
- **With sensitivity to conscience and weaker believers** — Romans 14; 1 Corinthians 8–10  

A concise summary verse is:

> **“For freedom Christ has set us free.” — Galatians 5:1**

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about marriage?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gen 2:24, Eph 5:22-33, Matt 19:4-6, Heb 13:4
questions.response:
The Bible teaches about marriage in many places. Here are some of the key passages:

## Foundational passages
- **Genesis 1:27–28** — God creates male and female and blesses them to be fruitful.
- **Genesis 2:18–24** — God creates marriage; a man and woman are joined and become “one flesh.”
- **Matthew 19:4–6** — Jesus quotes Genesis and teaches that marriage is God’s joining together.
- **Mark 10:6–9** — Parallel teaching of Jesus on marriage and “one flesh.”

## Love, faithfulness, and covenant
- **Malachi 2:14–16** — Marriage is described as a covenant, and God condemns unfaithfulness.
- **Proverbs 5:15–19** — Encourages delight and faithfulness within marriage.
- **Song of Solomon** — Celebrates marital love, affection, and desire.

## Husbands and wives
- **Ephesians 5:22–33** — Marriage is compared to Christ and the church; husbands are called to sacrificial love, wives to respect and submission.
- **Colossians 3:18–19** — Wives and husbands are instructed in their roles, with husbands commanded not to be harsh.
- **1 Peter 3:1–7** — Instructions to wives and husbands, including honor and understanding.
- **Titus 2:3–5** — Older women are to teach younger women about loving their husbands and families.

## Sexual purity and marital intimacy
- **Hebrews 13:4** — “Let marriage be held in honor among all,” and the marriage bed kept pure.
- **1 Corinthians 7:1–5** — Teaches about sexual relations within marriage and mutual responsibility.
- **1 Thessalonians 4:3–8** — Calls believers to sexual holiness.

## Singleness, marriage, and practical counsel
- **1 Corinthians 7** — Paul gives extensive teaching on marriage, singleness, divorce, widows, and remarriage.
- **Matthew 19:10–12** — Jesus speaks about singleness for the kingdom.
- **1 Timothy 5:14** — Paul gives practical counsel about younger widows remarrying.

## Divorce and remarriage
- **Deuteronomy 24:1–4** — Old Testament law concerning divorce.
- **Matthew 5:31–32** — Jesus teaches about divorce and adultery.
- **Matthew 19:3–9** — Jesus teaches that divorce was permitted because of hardness of heart, but God’s design is lifelong union.
- **Mark 10:2–12** — Jesus’ teaching on divorce and remarriage.
- **Luke 16:18** — Jesus’ warning about divorce and remarriage.
- **1 Corinthians 7:10–16** — Paul addresses separation, divorce, and marriage to an unbelieving spouse.

## Summary of the Bible’s teaching
The Bible presents marriage as a **God-designed covenant union** between a man and a woman, intended for companionship, faithfulness, love, sexual intimacy, family life, and reflecting God’s covenant love. It calls spouses to loyalty, purity, forgiveness, sacrificial love, and lifelong commitment.

questions.question: What passages address the role of the civil magistrate?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 13:1-7, 1 Pet 2:13-17, Acts 5:29, Dan 2:21
questions.response:
Key biblical passages addressing the role of the civil magistrate/civil authorities include:

- **Romans 13:1–7** — Civil authority is instituted by God; magistrates are to punish evil, approve good, and receive lawful taxes/customs.
- **1 Peter 2:13–17** — Governors are sent “to punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good”; Christians are to honor the emperor while fearing God.
- **Titus 3:1** — Believers are to be subject to rulers and authorities and ready for good works.
- **1 Timothy 2:1–2** — Christians should pray for kings and all in authority so that society may be peaceful and godly.
- **Matthew 22:21** — “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”
- **Acts 4:19–20; 5:29** — Civil obedience has limits: “We must obey God rather than men.”
- **Daniel 3; Daniel 6** — Examples of faithful disobedience when rulers command idolatry or forbid obedience to God.
- **Exodus 18:21–26** — Judges/rulers should be capable, God-fearing, trustworthy, and just.
- **Deuteronomy 16:18–20** — Magistrates/judges must judge with righteous judgment and not pervert justice.
- **2 Chronicles 19:5–7** — Judges are reminded that they judge for the Lord and must act with integrity.
- **Proverbs 8:15–16** — Kings and rulers govern under God’s providence.
- **Proverbs 29:4, 14** — Righteous rule establishes a land; justice toward the poor secures authority.
- **Psalm 72** — A model prayer for a ruler who governs with justice, protects the needy, and crushes oppressors.
- **Genesis 9:5–6** — Often cited as foundational for the magistrate’s role in restraining violence and upholding justice.
- **John 19:11** — Jesus tells Pilate that civil authority is given “from above,” showing its delegated nature.

In summary, these passages teach that civil magistrates are ordained by God to preserve public order, administer justice, punish wrongdoing, protect the innocent, and promote conditions in which people may live peaceably—while remaining subordinate to God’s higher authority.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "God elects individuals to salvation based on His foreknowledge of their future faith and repentance."
questions.reference_answer: Election is unconditional, not based on foreseen faith Faith is the result of election, not its cause

required_points: Election is unconditional, not based on foreseen faith
Faith is the result of election, not its cause
scoring.rubric: Must reject the Arminian view of conditional election based on foreseen faith. Should affirm unconditional election per Reformed standards.

questions.response:
From a **Reformed perspective**, the statement is rejected as an inadequate and unbiblical account of election.

> “God elects individuals to salvation based on His foreknowledge of their future faith and repentance.”

Reformed theology would say this describes **conditional election**—the idea that God chooses people because He foresees that they will believe and repent. That view is commonly associated with Arminian theology, not Reformed theology.

## 1. Reformed theology teaches unconditional election

In the Reformed view, God’s election is not based on anything foreseen in the individual—faith, repentance, works, moral quality, or spiritual responsiveness. Rather, election is grounded solely in God’s sovereign grace and good pleasure.

Key texts include:

- **Ephesians 1:4–5** — “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world… according to the purpose of his will.”
- **Romans 9:11–16** — God’s purpose in election stands “not because of works but because of him who calls.”
- **2 Timothy 1:9** — God saved us “not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace.”

So, from a Reformed perspective, God does not elect because He foresees faith; rather, He elects in order to bring about faith.

## 2. Faith and repentance are fruits of election, not the basis of it

Reformed theology affirms that believers are saved through faith and repentance. But it also insists that faith and repentance themselves are gifts of God’s grace.

- **Acts 13:48** — “As many as were appointed to eternal life believed.”
- **Philippians 1:29** — “It has been granted to you… to believe in him.”
- **Acts 11:18** — “God has granted repentance that leads to life.”

Therefore, faith is not the condition God foresees in order to elect someone. Faith is the result of God’s electing grace applied in time by the Holy Spirit.

## 3. “Foreknowledge” is understood relationally, not merely as foresight

Reformed interpreters often argue that biblical “foreknowledge” means more than God knowing future facts. It frequently carries the sense of God’s prior loving choice or covenantal regard.

For example:

- **Romans 8:29** — “Those whom he foreknew he also predestined…”
- **1 Peter 1:1–2** — believers are elect “according to the foreknowledge of God.”
- **Amos 3:2** — “You only have I known of all the families of the earth.”

In this sense, “foreknow” means something like “fore-loved” or “set His covenantal affection upon,” not merely “foresaw what they would do.”

## 4. The statement makes election dependent on human response

A Reformed critique would say that if God elects based on foreseen faith and repentance, then the decisive reason one person is saved and another is not lies ultimately in the human person. One believes and repents; another does not. Reformed theology sees this as undermining salvation by grace alone.

As the **Canons of Dort** put it, election is not based on “foreseen faith” or any “good quality or disposition” in the sinner, but solely on God’s gracious will.

## Conclusion

From a Reformed perspective, the statement is false or at least seriously misleading. God certainly foreknows all things, including who will believe and repent. But He does not elect people because He foresees their faith and repentance. Rather, He elects them by sovereign grace, and as a result He grants them faith, repentance, and perseverance in Christ.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "God's saving grace can be ultimately resisted by the free will of man."
questions.reference_answer: Effectual grace cannot be ultimately resisted God's sovereign call always accomplishes its purpose

required_points: Effectual grace cannot be ultimately resisted
God's sovereign call always accomplishes its purpose
scoring.rubric: Must reject the Arminian doctrine of resistible grace. Should affirm irresistible (effectual) grace.

questions.response:
From a Reformed perspective, the statement is **false or at least seriously misleading**, depending on what is meant by “saving grace.”

Reformed theology teaches that **God’s saving grace, when applied by the Holy Spirit to the elect, cannot be ultimately resisted**. This is often called **irresistible grace** or, more precisely, **effectual calling**.

The Reformed position does **not** mean that sinners never resist God in any sense. Scripture plainly says people resist the Holy Spirit and reject God’s Word outwardly, for example in Acts 7:51. People may resist sermons, warnings, convictions, and the external call of the gospel. In that sense, grace broadly considered can be resisted.

But Reformed theology distinguishes between:

1. **The external call** — the outward preaching of the gospel, which many resist.
2. **The internal/effectual call** — the sovereign work of the Holy Spirit by which God regenerates the elect and brings them willingly to faith in Christ.

The latter cannot finally fail.

Jesus says:

> “All that the Father gives me will come to me.”  
> — John 6:37

And again:

> “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.”  
> — John 6:44

From a Reformed view, this divine “drawing” is not mere persuasion that awaits man’s autonomous consent. It is a powerful, gracious work of God that changes the heart, renews the will, and causes the sinner to come freely and willingly to Christ.

The Westminster Confession says that those whom God effectually calls are:

> “enabled to answer this call, and to embrace the grace offered and conveyed in it.”  
> — Westminster Confession of Faith 10.2

So Reformed theology does affirm that humans make real choices. The sinner who comes to Christ does so willingly, not by coercion. But because of total depravity, fallen man’s will is bound by sin and will not choose Christ apart from regenerating grace. When God gives saving grace, He liberates the will so that the sinner freely comes to Christ.

Therefore, a Reformed evaluation would be:

**If “saving grace” means God’s effectual, regenerating grace toward the elect, then it cannot be ultimately resisted by man’s free will. God’s grace triumphs, not by violating the will, but by renewing it.**

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "A truly regenerate believer can fall away from grace and lose their salvation."
questions.reference_answer: True believers cannot lose salvation God preserves the elect

required_points: True believers cannot lose salvation
God preserves the elect
scoring.rubric: Must reject the possibility of losing salvation. Should affirm the perseverance and preservation of the saints.

questions.response:
From a Reformed perspective, the statement is **false** as written.

Reformed theology teaches the **perseverance of the saints**: those whom God has truly regenerated, effectually called, justified, and united to Christ will be preserved by God and will persevere in faith to the end. A truly regenerate believer may fall into serious sin, experience seasons of spiritual coldness, or lose assurance for a time, but cannot finally and totally fall away from grace and lose salvation.

Key Reformed convictions include:

- **Salvation is grounded in God’s sovereign grace**, not ultimately in human willpower.  
- **Regeneration is effectual**: God gives new life that will not finally be undone.  
- **Christ preserves His sheep**: “No one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28).  
- **God completes what He begins**: “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6).  
- **Those justified will be glorified** (Romans 8:30), indicating an unbreakable chain of salvation.

Reformed theology also takes seriously biblical warnings about apostasy, such as Hebrews 6 and Hebrews 10. However, it understands these warnings as real means God uses to keep His people persevering. When someone permanently abandons Christ, the Reformed view is that this reveals they were never truly regenerate, even if they once professed faith or participated in the visible church. As 1 John 2:19 says:

> “They went out from us, but they were not of us.”

The Westminster Confession expresses the classic Reformed position:

> “They, whom God hath accepted in his Beloved… can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace; but shall certainly persevere therein to the end, and be eternally saved.”  
> — Westminster Confession of Faith 17.1

So, from a Reformed perspective, a better statement would be:

> A truly regenerate believer may grievously sin and temporarily lose assurance, but by God’s preserving grace will not finally fall away or lose salvation. Final apostasy reveals an unregenerate heart rather than the loss of true regeneration.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "Christ died equally for every individual person, intending to save all without distinction."
questions.reference_answer: The atonement is particular and definite Christ died especially for the elect

required_points: The atonement is particular and definite
Christ died especially for the elect
scoring.rubric: Must reject universal atonement in intent. Should affirm particular redemption while acknowledging sufficiency for all.

questions.response:
From a **Reformed** perspective, the statement is at best **ambiguous** and, as worded, is generally **rejected**.

### 1. “Christ died equally for every individual person”
Classic Reformed theology denies that Christ died for every person in the same saving sense. Reformed doctrine teaches **definite atonement** or **particular redemption**: Christ’s death was intended to actually redeem the elect, not merely make salvation possible for all.

Christ’s death is of **infinite worth** and therefore **sufficient for all**, but it is **efficient for the elect**.

The Canons of Dort say Christ’s death is “of infinite value and worth, more than sufficient to atone for the sins of the whole world,” but that God intended through it to “effectually redeem” the elect.

### 2. “Intending to save all”
If this means that God had the same saving intention toward every individual, Reformed theology rejects that. God’s saving decree is particular: he chose a people in Christ and sent Christ to secure their salvation.

In Reformed thought, Christ does not merely make people savable; he actually purchases redemption, faith, repentance, and final salvation for those given to him by the Father.

### 3. “Without distinction”
This phrase can be understood in two ways.

If it means **all kinds of people** — Jews and Gentiles, rich and poor, men and women, people from every nation — then Reformed theology gladly affirms it. Christ saves people from every tribe, tongue, people, and nation.

But if it means **every individual without exception**, then the statement conflicts with definite atonement.

### 4. What Reformed theology does affirm
A Reformed formulation would be:

> Christ’s death is sufficient for all and should be proclaimed freely to all. God genuinely commands all people to repent and believe. Yet Christ died with a definite saving purpose for the elect, securing their redemption infallibly.

So, from a Reformed perspective, the original statement should be qualified. Christ did not die “equally” for every individual with the same intent to save each one. Rather, he died effectually for his people, while the gospel is sincerely offered to all without distinction.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "God gives prevenient grace to all people, enabling them to freely choose or reject salvation."
questions.reference_answer: Prevenient grace as an enabling universal gift is not a Reformed doctrine Effectual grace is particular, not universal

required_points: Prevenient grace as an enabling universal gift is not a Reformed doctrine
Effectual grace is particular, not universal
scoring.rubric: Must reject the Arminian doctrine of prevenient grace. Should distinguish effectual calling from a universal enabling grace.

questions.response:
From a Reformed perspective, the statement is generally rejected as an Arminian/Wesleyan formulation rather than a Reformed one.

> “God gives prevenient grace to all people, enabling them to freely choose or reject salvation.”

## 1. Reformed theology affirms human inability apart from grace

Reformed theology teaches that because of total depravity, fallen human beings are not morally able to choose Christ savingly on their own.

This does not mean people are as evil as possible, or that they lack a will. Rather, it means that apart from regenerating grace, the human will is bound by sin and will not desire God rightly.

Key texts often cited include:

- “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” — John 6:44  
- “The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God” — 1 Corinthians 2:14  
- “You were dead in the trespasses and sins” — Ephesians 2:1  
- “No one seeks for God” — Romans 3:11  

So Reformed theology denies that all people receive a universal grace that restores their ability to make a neutral, libertarian free choice for or against Christ.

## 2. Reformed theology distinguishes common grace from saving grace

Reformed theology does affirm that God gives grace to all people in some sense. This is often called common grace.

Common grace includes things like:

- restraint of evil,
- blessings of creation,
- moral awareness,
- providential kindness,
- exposure to truth,
- the general call of the gospel.

But common grace does not savingly enable every person to believe. It does not overcome spiritual deadness or guarantee the moral ability to embrace Christ.

So a Reformed theologian may say God shows real kindness and patience toward all, but would not usually say God gives “prevenient grace” to all in the Wesleyan sense.

## 3. Reformed theology affirms effectual grace for the elect

Instead of universal prevenient grace, Reformed theology teaches effectual calling or irresistible grace.

That means God not only outwardly calls sinners through the gospel, but inwardly and effectually calls the elect by the Holy Spirit, bringing them from spiritual death to life.

This grace does not merely make salvation possible; it actually brings the sinner to faith.

As Jesus says:

> “All that the Father gives me will come to me” — John 6:37

And Paul writes:

> “Those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified” — Romans 8:30

In Reformed theology, regeneration precedes and produces saving faith. The sinner freely comes to Christ, but only because God has first changed the heart.

## 4. The Reformed objection to the statement

The main Reformed objections would be:

1. It implies that grace merely enables rather than effectually saves.  
2. It assumes all people receive the same saving enablement.  
3. It makes the decisive difference between salvation and damnation lie in the human will rather than God’s electing grace.  
4. It conflicts with the Reformed understanding of total depravity and unconditional election.

From a Reformed perspective, if two sinners both receive prevenient grace and one believes while the other rejects Christ, then the ultimate explanation for salvation appears to be something in the believer — his wiser, better, or more willing response. Reformed theology sees that as compromising salvation by grace alone.

## 5. A Reformed restatement

A Reformed version would be:

> God commands all people to repent and believe the gospel. Through the outward call, he sincerely offers Christ to sinners. Yet because of human depravity, no one will come to Christ unless God effectually calls and regenerates him by the Holy Spirit. This saving grace is given to the elect and unfailingly brings them to faith.

So, from a Reformed perspective, the statement is not acceptable if “prevenient grace” means a universal, resistible grace that restores free will equally to all. Reformed theology instead affirms common grace to all, the general gospel call to all, and effectual saving grace to the elect.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "Man has libertarian free will that allows him to choose between good and evil apart from God's determining will."
questions.reference_answer: Fallen man's will is in bondage to sin True freedom comes through regeneration

required_points: Fallen man's will is in bondage to sin
True freedom comes through regeneration
scoring.rubric: Must reject libertarian free will in the fallen state. Should affirm compatibilist freedom and the bondage of the will.

questions.response:
From a Reformed perspective, the statement is **rejected** as inconsistent with biblical teaching on God’s sovereignty, human nature, and grace.

> “Man has libertarian free will that allows him to choose between good and evil apart from God's determining will.”

### 1. Reformed theology rejects libertarian free will

Libertarian free will usually means that a person’s choices are not determined by God, nature, desires, or prior causes, and that the person could choose otherwise in an ultimate, self-determining sense.

Reformed theology does not affirm this. It teaches that human beings make real, voluntary choices, but those choices are governed by their nature, desires, and ultimately by God’s sovereign decree.

The Westminster Confession says:

> “God from all eternity did, by the most wise and holy counsel of His own will, freely and unchangeably ordain whatsoever comes to pass.”  
> — Westminster Confession of Faith 3.1

So nothing happens “apart from God’s determining will.”

### 2. Man is morally responsible, but not autonomous

Reformed theology affirms that man truly chooses. People are not robots or externally coerced machines. They act willingly and are responsible for their actions.

However, Reformed theology denies that man is autonomous or independent of God’s decree. Human choices are real, but they occur within God’s sovereign providence.

A classic Reformed view is often called **compatibilism**: God sovereignly ordains all things, and human beings still make genuine voluntary choices for which they are morally accountable.

For example, Joseph’s brothers freely sinned against him, yet Joseph says:

> “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.”  
> — Genesis 50:20

Their evil intention was real, but God’s sovereign purpose was also real and supreme.

### 3. Fallen man cannot choose spiritual good apart from grace

Reformed theology also emphasizes the bondage of the will after the Fall. Fallen man can make ordinary choices and even perform outwardly good actions, but he cannot choose God savingly apart from regenerating grace.

Scripture says:

> “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.”  
> — John 6:44

And:

> “The mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God… it cannot submit to God.”  
> — Romans 8:7

Therefore, fallen man does not possess a neutral ability to choose either good or evil in the deepest spiritual sense. Apart from grace, he freely chooses according to his sinful nature.

### 4. God’s sovereignty does not make Him the author of sin

Reformed theology carefully distinguishes between God’s sovereign ordination of all things and His moral approval of evil. God decrees whatsoever comes to pass, including even sinful actions, but He does so in such a way that He is not the author of sin and does not violate the will of creatures.

The Westminster Confession continues:

> “Yet so, as thereby neither is God the author of sin, nor is violence offered to the will of the creatures.”  
> — Westminster Confession of Faith 3.1

The crucifixion of Christ is the clearest example:

> “This Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed.”  
> — Acts 2:23

The crucifixion was ordained by God, yet those who committed it were responsible for their evil actions.

### Conclusion

From a Reformed perspective, the statement is false. Man does not possess libertarian free will that operates independently of God’s determining will. Rather, man has a real and responsible will, but it is always subject to God’s sovereign decree. Fallen man freely chooses according to his sinful nature and cannot choose spiritual good apart from God’s regenerating grace. God ordains all things, yet human beings remain morally accountable for their voluntary choices.

It uses relevant Scripture and Confessional citations.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "The Pope, when speaking ex cathedra on matters of faith and morals, is infallible and his teachings are irreformable."
questions.reference_answer: No human being is infallible Scripture alone is the infallible rule of faith

required_points: No human being is infallible
Scripture alone is the infallible rule of faith
scoring.rubric: Must reject papal infallibility. Should affirm Sola Scriptura as the only infallible rule.

questions.response:
From a Reformed perspective, the statement is rejected.

The Roman Catholic doctrine, formally defined at Vatican I, teaches that the pope is infallible when he speaks *ex cathedra*—that is, in his official capacity as supreme pastor of the church, defining doctrine concerning faith or morals to be held by the whole church. Such teachings are said to be “irreformable of themselves.”

Reformed theology disagrees on several grounds:

1. **Scripture alone is the only infallible rule of faith and life**  
   Reformed theology holds to *sola Scriptura*: Scripture is the final, sufficient, and infallible authority for the church. Church officers, councils, synods, and traditions have real but subordinate authority. They may teach truly, but they are not inherently infallible.

2. **Only Christ is the supreme head of the church**  
   The Reformed tradition denies that the pope has universal jurisdiction over the church. Christ alone is the church’s head, and he governs his people by his Word and Spirit.

3. **Church leaders and councils can err**  
   The Westminster Confession of Faith says:

   > “All synods or councils, since the Apostles’ times, whether general or particular, may err; and many have erred.”  
   > —WCF 31.3

   Therefore, no post-apostolic church authority, including the pope, can issue teachings that are automatically infallible or irreformable.

4. **Apostolic authority was unique and foundational**  
   Reformed theology distinguishes between the apostles, who were uniquely commissioned by Christ and inspired by the Holy Spirit, and later church officers. The pope is not viewed as possessing the apostolic authority of Peter, nor as Peter’s infallible successor.

5. **Doctrines must always be tested by Scripture**  
   Any teaching on faith or morals must be examined according to the written Word of God. If a pope, council, or church confession contradicts Scripture, Reformed theology says it must be rejected or reformed.

So, from a Reformed perspective, the statement is false. The pope is not infallible, even when speaking *ex cathedra*, and no papal teaching is irreformable simply because it comes from the pope. The only irreformable and infallible authority for the church is God speaking in Holy Scripture.

questions.question: Evaluate this statement from a Reformed perspective: "Justification involves an infusion of righteousness that makes the believer inherently righteous before God."
questions.reference_answer: Justification is a legal declaration, not an infusion Christ's righteousness is imputed, not infused

required_points: Justification is a legal declaration, not an infusion
Christ's righteousness is imputed, not infused
scoring.rubric: Must reject the Roman Catholic doctrine of infused righteousness. Should affirm forensic justification by imputed righteousness.

questions.response:
From a Reformed perspective, the statement is **incorrect** or at least seriously confused.

Reformed theology teaches that **justification is not an infusion of righteousness into the believer**, but a **forensic/legal declaration** by God that the sinner is righteous on the basis of Christ’s righteousness **imputed** to him and received by faith alone.

### Reformed view of justification

In justification, God:

1. **pardons the believer’s sins**, and  
2. **counts or imputes Christ’s righteousness to the believer**.

The believer is therefore righteous **before God**, not because he has become inherently righteous in himself, but because he is united to Christ and clothed in Christ’s righteousness.

Key language often used in Reformed theology:

- **Imputed righteousness**, not infused righteousness.
- **Alien righteousness** — righteousness belonging properly to Christ, credited to the believer.
- **Forensic justification** — a legal declaration, not an inward moral transformation.
- **Faith alone** — faith receives Christ and his righteousness; it does not itself become the ground of justification.

### Infusion belongs to sanctification, not justification

Reformed theology does affirm that God inwardly renews believers and makes them increasingly holy. But that belongs to **sanctification**, not justification.

So the Reformed distinction is:

- **Justification**: God declares the believer righteous because of Christ’s righteousness imputed to him.
- **Sanctification**: God progressively makes the believer righteous in character and conduct by the Spirit.

The statement confuses these two doctrines by making justification depend on an inward transformation.

### Contrast with Roman Catholic theology

The language of an “infusion of righteousness” is more characteristic of Roman Catholic theology, especially as articulated at the Council of Trent. In that view, justification includes the inward renewal of the person, so that righteousness is infused and the believer becomes inherently righteous.

The Reformed tradition rejects that as undermining the sufficiency of Christ’s righteousness and the assurance of justification by faith alone.

### Better Reformed formulation

A Reformed version would be:

> Justification is God’s gracious act of declaring sinners righteous on the basis of the righteousness of Christ imputed to them and received by faith alone.

So, from a Reformed perspective, the original statement should be rejected because **justification does not make the believer inherently righteous; it declares the believer righteous in Christ.**
